The deck builds up in one direction: first what it means for two devices to exchange data, then how many devices are wired together (connections and topologies), then how big a network is (LAN, MAN, WAN), and finally how all those networks join into the Internet through ISPs, and why everyone has to agree on standards for any of it to work. Tutorial 1 was written from this deck, so its questions show what the instructor checks: definitions (what a protocol is), recognising a mode or topology from a description, counting links with the formulas, and scenario questions where you pick a topology and justify it. Data Communications

Data communication is the smallest picture in the course: two devices exchanging information over a transmission medium . The medium is whatever physically carries the signal: a copper cable, a glass fibre, or radio waves through the air. Everything else in the course (networks, the Internet) is many of these two-device exchanges put together. For it to be useful, the data must arrive at the right device, arrive correctly, and arrive on time. Five components of data communication (Figure 1.1)

Learn the five as answers to five questions. What is sent? The message. Who sends it? The sender. Who gets it? The receiver. Over what ? The transmission medium. Following which rules ? The protocol. If an exam option names a device such as a router or switch, it is not one of the five: those are network devices, not parts of the basic model. The figure draws the protocol box on both sides because a protocol only works if both ends follow the same rules. Two people can share a phone line (same medium) and still fail to communicate if one speaks Arabic and the other only Japanese: the medium connected them, but there was no shared protocol. That is the difference between the medium (the path) and the protocol (the agreement). “My Sister Reads The Paper”: Message, Sender, Receiver, Transmission medium, Protocol. The medium is the physical path. The protocol is the set of rules. Don’t swap them. 1.1.2 Message

A network can only carry bits, so every kind of information is turned into bits first. Text is stored as a bit pattern using a code such as Unicode (each character gets a number, and the number is sent in binary). Numbers are converted directly to binary . Images are a grid of pixels, and each pixel becomes a bit pattern (1 bit for black and white, more bits for colour). Audio is sound, which is continuous, so it is sampled into numbers. Video is many images shown quickly one after another (plus audio). The exam point: the form differs, but on the medium it is all bits. 1.2 Networks

A node is any device on the network. It can be a host , a device people actually use (computer, printer, phone), or a networking device whose job is to move data (router, switch, modem). A link is the pathway between two nodes, and it can be a cable or a wireless channel. So a network is just nodes plus links. There are only two ways to use a link. Point-to-point : the link joins exactly two devices, and its full capacity belongs to them. Multipoint (also called multidrop): more than two devices share one link, so they must share its capacity, either at the same time (spatially) or by taking turns (temporally). Sharing is cheaper, but it means devices can get in each other’s way, which is why Chapter 3 needs multiple-access protocols. A network is judged on three criteria. Performance asks how fast: it is measured by throughput (how much data actually gets through per second) and delay (transit time across the network, and response time to a request). It depends on the number of users, the medium, the hardware and the software. Reliability asks how dependable: it is measured by the frequency of failure and the time a link takes to recover from one. Security asks how protected: keeping out unauthorised users, preventing damage to data, and having policies to recover from breaches and data loss. A common trap is mixing up the measures: failure frequency is reliability, not performance. More throughput and less delay pull against each other: pushing more data in raises the delay. Criteria = “PRS”: Performance, Reliability, Security. Multipoint means one link, more than two devices. The figure shows a mainframe and three workstations hanging off a single cable. Data flow (direction of data flowing in the link) (Figure 1.2)

Simplex : data only ever travels in one direction, like a one-way street. One device only sends and the other only receives. Examples: a keyboard sending to a computer, a monitor receiving from it, a radio broadcast. The receiver can never answer on that channel. Half-duplex : both devices can send, but not at the same time . They take turns, and whoever is sending gets the entire capacity of the channel. A walkie-talkie is the standard example: you press the button, speak, say “over”, and only then can the other person reply. If both press at once, neither gets through. Full-duplex : both devices send and receive at the same time , like a phone call where both people can talk at once. The catch is that the channel’s capacity is shared between the two directions all the time, either because the link has two separate paths (one per direction) or because the capacity is divided. Tutorial 1 asks exactly this: “capacity shared by both directions at all times” means full-duplex. Half-duplex = “over” on a walkie-talkie. Full-duplex = talking over each other on the phone. Categories of topology (Figure 1.7)

Topology is the shape of the network: how the devices and links are physically arranged, or how devices are interconnected. It matters because the shape decides how much cable you need, what happens when something breaks, and how easy it is to add a device. Each topology on the next slides is a different trade-off between cost and robustness. There are four basic topologies: mesh (everyone linked to everyone), star (everyone linked to a centre), bus (everyone on one shared cable) and ring (everyone linked to two neighbours in a loop). Real networks often combine them, which is called a hybrid topology (slide 15). Four topologies: “My Star Bus Rings” (Mesh, Star, Bus, Ring). Fully connected mesh topology (for five devices) (Figure 1.8)

In a fully connected mesh every device has its own dedicated link to every other device. To count the links: each of the N devices connects to the other N-1, which gives N(N-1), but that counts every link twice (A to B and B to A are the same cable), so divide by 2: N(N-1)/2 . Each device needs one I/O port (one NIC) per link it has, so N-1 ports per device . Example: 5 devices need 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 links and 4 ports each. Why is mesh expensive ? Because the number of cables and ports grows roughly with the square of the number of devices: 10 devices need 45 links, 50 devices need 1,225. Every link is a cable to buy, install and maintain, which is also why it is hard to install and update. What you get for that cost: dedicated links mean no traffic problems and better privacy (nobody else sees your link), a broken link only affects the two devices on it, and faults are easy to find. That is why mesh is used where reliability matters most, such as backbone links between main routers. N = 8 → 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 links, 7 ports per device. Ports per device is N-1, not N(N-1)/2. Star topology (Figure 1.9)

In a star, each device has a dedicated point-to-point link only to the central controller (a hub or switch), never directly to another device. To send from A to B, the data goes A to the hub, then hub to B. That is why it needs only N links for N devices, one per device, and each device needs only one port. It is cheaper than mesh, easy to install, and adding or removing a device means plugging one cable into the hub. Star is called robust because if one cable breaks, only the device on that cable is cut off; everyone else keeps working, and the broken link is easy to identify. But the whole network depends on the centre: if the hub or switch fails, nothing works . That is called a single point of failure. In exam answers, mention both: robust against link failures, not against hub failure. Robust ≠ fault-proof: one bad link only takes out its device, but the hub failing takes out everything. Bus topology (Figure 1.10)

A bus is one long cable, called the backbone or main cable, running past all the devices. Each device connects to it through a short drop line attached with a tap . So for N devices you need 1 main cable + N drop lines . Signals travel along the whole backbone and every device hears every transmission. The ends of the cable need terminators so the signal doesn’t bounce back. Bus needs less cable than mesh or star because the backbone can take the most efficient route. The weakness is the shared backbone. A single break in the main cable stops all transmission , because the signal can no longer pass and it reflects off the break. Faults are hard to isolate since one cable serves everybody, and adding devices is hard because each tap weakens the signal and the backbone has a limited length. This is why the old shared-cable Ethernet LANs were replaced by star (switched) LANs. Formulas for N devices: mesh N(N-1)/2 links and N-1 ports each · star N links · ring N links · bus 1 main cable + N drop lines. Ring topology (Figure 1.11)

In a ring, each device has a dedicated point-to-point link to exactly two neighbours , one on each side, forming a closed loop, so N devices need N links . Data travels around the ring in one direction, passing from device to device. Each device contains a repeater that regenerates the signal and passes it on if the data isn’t addressed to it. Faults are easy to find: if a device stops getting a signal within the expected time, it raises an alarm, so the break is located quickly. Ring is not robust : since data must travel around the loop, one broken link or one failed device can stop the whole ring (in a simple, one-direction ring). The usual fix is a dual ring , a second loop that runs in the other direction and takes over when the first one breaks. Compare with star: in a star, a broken cable cuts off one device; in a ring, it can cut off everyone. A ring of 12 devices needs how many links? Fault isolation is easy in a ring topology. What is the main disadvantage of a simple ring? What does the repeater in each ring device do? A hybrid topology: a star backbone with bus or ring networks

A hybrid topology combines two or more basic ones. The figure shows a star backbone : a central device connects several bus segments (star-bus) or several rings (star-ring). This is how real organisations grow: each department may have its own small network, and a central device ties them together. In an exam, if a description mixes two shapes, the answer is hybrid. Categories of networks (Figure 1.12)

Networks are also classified by geographic size . A LAN (local area network) covers a room, a building or a campus, up to about a kilometre, and is usually privately owned. A MAN (metropolitan area network) covers a town or city, around 10 km. A WAN (wide area network) covers a country, a continent or the whole world. The figure’s table runs from 1 m (a personal area network) to 10,000 km (the Internet). Tutorial 1 tests this with a true/false: “A LAN typically covers an area larger than 2 miles” is false . A LAN is limited to a few kilometres at most, so if a network spans a whole city it is a MAN, and between cities or countries it is a WAN. An isolated LAN in the past and today (Figure 1.8)

The figure contrasts two ways of building the same LAN. In the past , all hosts were attached to one shared cable , which is a bus: only one host could send at a time, and a cable break took down everyone. Today , each host has its own cable to a switch , which is a star: the switch forwards each frame only to the host it is meant for, so hosts no longer compete for one cable. This shift (shared bus to switched star) comes back in Chapter 4 on Ethernet. An internetwork , or internet with a small i, is what you get when two or more networks are connected , using routers at the joins. WAN (Figure 1.15)

A WAN provides long-distance transmission: between cities, countries and continents. LANs are usually owned by the organisation using them, while WAN links are usually leased from telecom companies. WANs are often built as a mesh (or partial mesh) of point-to-point links between sites, because a mesh gives each pair of sites its own link and keeps working when one link fails. 1.3 The Internet

The Internet is a collection of many different networks, LANs and WANs, joined by connecting devices and switching stations, that all run the TCP/IP protocol suite. TCP/IP is what makes it one Internet rather than many separate networks: it is the common language every connected network agrees to speak. For a host to count as being on the Internet , it needs three things: it must run TCP/IP , it must have an Internet (IP) address so others can reach it, and it must be able to send IP packets to other machines on the Internet. A computer on a private network with no IP route out is not on the Internet, even if it runs TCP/IP internally. Internet Service Providers (ISPs)

ISPs are arranged in tiers. Tier 1 ISPs are the backbones of the Internet: international, very few of them, they own their own links and routers across continents, and they connect directly to each other , so they never pay anyone to reach the rest of the Internet. Examples: Sprint, AT&T, Lumen. Tier 3 ISPs are local ISPs . They don’t have international links of their own; they take service from the national providers and sell access to homes and businesses. So traffic from your laptop typically climbs tier 3, tier 2, tier 1 and back down to reach a server abroad. Tier number goes UP as you get closer to the customer: 1 = global, 2 = national, 3 = local. STC and Mobily are examples of: Tier-1 ISPs connect directly to other tier-1 ISPs. A local ISP that buys its Internet access from a national provider is: Which describes a tier-1 ISP? Internet structure: network of networks

The Internet is a network of networks . Tier-1 ISPs sit in the centre and connect to each other; tier-2 ISPs connect to tier 1; local and tier-3 ISPs connect to tier 2 and are its customers. The access network is the last hop: the link that connects the end systems (your home router, your phone) to their local ISP. No single organisation owns the whole thing. Methods of ISPs InterConnection

Peering is the interconnection of two networks so they can exchange traffic directly. Without peering, two ISPs could only reach each other through some third network. The slide gives two ways to peer. Private peering is a direct connection between ISPs. The peering points are a group of routers owned and operated by the ISPs themselves , not by a third-party company. An Internet Exchange Point (IXP) is public peering: a physical facility managed by a third party , built from high-speed switching networks, where any ISP can connect with any other . IXPs carry enormous amounts of traffic. The current trend: international ISPs (tier 1) connect to each other at private peering points , while national ISPs interconnect using IXPs . The trap in exams is who runs what: private peering points are run by the ISPs; an IXP is run by a third party. Private peering points are run by the ISPs; an IXP is run by a THIRD party. 1.4 Internet Standards

In the early 1970s, IBM, Digital Equipment and other vendors each built their own networking architecture that only worked with their own computers. A company with IBM machines and DEC machines could not connect them without major translation software . The problem this created is the reason standards exist: devices from different makers have to agree on common rules. A protocol is a set of rules that controls how data is exchanged between two entities. An entity is anything that can send and receive information, such as an application (an email program, a browser). A system is the physical machine it runs on (a computer, a terminal, a remote sensor). Tutorial 1’s trap: “A protocol is the structure or format of the data” is false , because format (syntax) is only one part of a protocol; a protocol also covers meaning (semantics) and timing. “A protocol is the structure or format of the data” ✗. Internet Standards

Standards are agreed protocols published so that everyone can follow them. They specify the hardware and software procedures so computers can talk to each other correctly and reliably , and their main purpose is interoperability : equipment from different vendors working together. Without standards, a Dell laptop could only talk to a Dell router. The benefits: standards create a large market (a vendor can sell to everyone, which lowers prices), give guidelines to manufacturers, vendors and government agencies, and let products from different vendors communicate . The list at the bottom shows how many separate things must be agreed: how many volts mean 0 or 1, where a message ends, what to do with lost messages, how big each data type is, how machines are identified, how to find a route to a machine, and how applications talk. Each of these questions becomes a job for one layer in Part 2. Know each organisation by what it covers. ISO is the international body (it made the OSI model). ITU-T is the United Nations agency for telecommunications standards. ANSI is the United States national standards body. IEEE focuses on LAN and MAN standards, for example 802.3 (Ethernet) and 802.11 (Wi-Fi). W3C sets the standards for the World Wide Web (HTML, CSS). If a question says LAN or MAN standards, the answer is IEEE. Ch 4, slide 3 : IEEE 802 LAN standards Which organization specializes in LAN/MAN standards? n: Introduction

The whole deck answers one question: how do you organise something as complicated as a network? The answer is layers . You meet the idea first, then the OSI model (7 layers), then how data is wrapped and unwrapped as it moves through them ( encapsulation ), then what each layer does, which unit of data (PDU) it handles and which address it uses, and finally the TCP/IP model (5 layers) that the Internet actually runs. The table on slide 51 (layer, job, PDU, address) is the most reused thing in the course. Chapter 2 is the physical layer, Chapters 3 to 6 are the data link layer, Chapters 7 and 8 are the network layer, Chapter 9 is transport and Chapter 10 is application. If you know the table, you always know where a new topic sits. Chapter 01 Introduction Data Communications ■ and Networking, With TCP/IP protocol suite Sixth Edition Behrouz A. Chapter 1-Part 2: Outline

Three sections: 1.4 protocol layering (why layers, how layers talk), 1.5 the TCP/IP suite and 1.6 the OSI model . The slides actually teach OSI first and then show how TCP/IP maps onto it, so read them in that order. Chapter 1-Part 2: Outline 1.4 PROTOCOL LAYERING ■ 1.5 TCP/IP PROTOCOL SUITE ■ 1.6 THE OSI MODEL ■ 2
Protocol Layers and Service Models

A network involves cables, signals, addresses, routes, error checks, applications and much more. If one program had to handle all of it, nobody could build it, understand it or fix it. The question on the slide is how developers and users can cope with that complexity. The solution is to split the work into layers . A layer is a logical grouping of related functions: one layer only worries about turning bits into signals, another only about finding a route, another only about getting a whole message to the right program. Each layer solves one part of the problem and trusts the others to do theirs, and the layers exist on every node in the network. Layers are stacked, and each one uses the services of the layer below and provides a service to the layer above : layer n-1 serves layer n. The meeting point between two neighbouring layers is called the interface . It defines exactly what information, operations and services the lower layer offers the upper one, like a menu. As long as the interface stays the same, a layer’s inside can be changed without affecting anyone else. A layer only talks to the one directly above and below it on the same machine. The boundary between two adjacent layers is called a(n): In a layered architecture, layer n-1 provides a service to layer n. Why are network functions designed as layers? Protocol Layers and Service Models Computer network architecture is complex ■ Too many components ■ How to understand its architecture? ■ How to allow developers and users to deal with this complexity? ■ Solution 🡺 ■ Computer networks functions are designed and implemented as ■ layers Layers are logical groupings of all the processes or functions ■ required for effective data exchange Layer n-1 provides some service to the layer n through a well- ■ defined interface (boundary between each two layers) Each interface defines what information, operations, and ■ services a layer must provide for the layer above it. These layers are distributed across all nodes in the network ■
Layers, protocols, and interfaces

Read the figure in two directions. Horizontally , layer 3 on host 1 follows the same rules as layer 3 on host 2: those rules are the layer-3 protocol , and the two layer-3s are called peers . Vertically , each layer hands data to the layer directly below it on the same host through an interface . So: protocol = between the same layer on different machines; interface = between adjacent layers on the same machine. The peers never actually send anything directly to each other. Layer 3 on host 1 passes its data down to layer 2, then to layer 1, and only layer 1 puts signals on the physical medium . On host 2 the data goes back up. The horizontal conversation is logical (it feels direct to the layer), while the real path is down, across and up. Protocol ≠ interface. A protocol is between peers on different machines; an interface is between neighbours on the same machine. Rules used between the same layer on two different hosts are a: Layer 3 on host 1 sends its data directly across the medium to layer 3 on host 2. Layers, protocols, and interfaces.
Communication through an internet

Not every device on the path needs every layer. The hosts (source A and destination B) use all five , because the data starts and ends in an application. A link-layer switch only uses layers 1 and 2 : it reads the frame’s MAC address and forwards the frame on the same network. A router uses layers 1 to 3 : it reads the IP address to decide which network to send the packet to next. Neither looks at the transport or application data. The more layers a device implements, the more work and processing it does, so the more complex it is. A host is the most complex, a router is in the middle, a switch is simpler, and a repeater or hub (layer 1 only) is the simplest. This ranking comes back in Chapter 6 on connecting devices. Ch 6, slide 3 : Which layer each connecting device works at Up to which layer does a router operate? A link-layer switch uses which layers? Which device is the most complex in terms of layers? Figure 1.18 Communication through an internet ▪ Some devices do not use all layers. ▪ Complexity of an entity increases with the number of layers that it supports
Advantages of Layered Architecture

The first advantage is simplicity : one huge, complicated process becomes several smaller, simpler ones, so the hardware and software for each layer are easier to implement and easier to test and fix. The second advantage comes from two rules: each layer has its own distinct set of protocols (no two layers do the same job), and there is a well-defined interface between neighbouring layers. Together these mean each layer can be built independently . A network card maker can build layers 1 and 2, an operating system maker layers 3 and 4, a browser maker layer 7, and the result still works because each respects the interfaces. That lets different manufacturers work on different layers, which encourages both collaboration and competition. Give two advantages of a layered network architecture. Why can a NIC from one company work with an operating system from another? Advantages of Layered Architecture Breaks the complicated communication process into layers of ■ simpler processes which allows easier hardware or software implementation Each layer implements distinct (different from other layers ■ and unique) set of protocols (functions), and Well-defined interface between layers n and n-1 ■ The advantage of the above two requirements: ■ The implementation of each layer can be done ■ independently of the other layers. This allows different manufacturers to supply the ■ hardware and software needed to the different layers 🡺 encourages collaboration & Competition
Standard Protocol Models

The set of protocols used by all the layers together is called a protocol stack , because the protocols are stacked one above the other, like the layers. There are two standard stacks. OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) is the 7-layer reference model from ISO; it is mainly used to teach and discuss networking. TCP/IP is the suite the Internet actually runs. You need both: OSI for the vocabulary (people still say “layer 7” or “a layer-3 switch”), and TCP/IP for what really happens. The set of protocols used by all the layers is called: Which two standard protocol models does the slide name? Standard Protocol Models The protocols of the various layers are called protocol stack ■ Two Standard Protocol models (stack) exist: ■ Open System Interconnect (OSI) ■ Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) ■
OSI Model

OSI stands for Open Systems Interconnection. It was developed by ISO , the International Organization for Standardization, in the 1970s, as a framework for standardising networks. An open system is a set of protocols that lets any two systems communicate regardless of their underlying architecture : an IBM machine and a Mac can talk as long as both follow the model. The model describes how data moves from an application on one computer to an application on another. It dominated before 1990, after which TCP/IP took over in practice. Watch the letters: ISO is the organisation, OSI is the model. ISO is the organization, OSI is the model. Exam options often swap them. The OSI model was developed by: What is an “open system” in the OSI sense? OSI Model Developed by ISO ( ■ the International Organization for in 1970s Standardization) Provides framework for standardization ■ An open system is a set of protocols that ■ allow any two different systems to communicate regardless of their underlying architecture. Describes how data and network ■ information moves from an application in one computer to an application in another computer. Dominated before 1990 ■
OSI Model

Number the layers from the bottom: 1 Physical , 2 Data link , 3 Network , 4 Transport , 5 Session , 6 Presentation , 7 Application . Exams ask both ways: “which layer is number 4?” (transport) and “which layer is above the network layer?” (transport). Being able to count up and down the stack quickly saves time on every later chapter. Which OSI layer number is the transport layer? Which layer sits directly above the network layer in OSI? Which OSI layer is number 6? OSI Model
OSI Model

The slide’s sentence goes top-down : A ll P eople S eem T o N eed D ata P rocessing gives Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical. If you prefer counting from layer 1 upwards, use the bottom-up sentence in the tip below. Bottom-up version: “Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away”. In “All People Seem To Need Data Processing”, what does the “S” stand for? OSI Model To remember the 7 layers is the sentence “All people seem to need data processing”
OSI Protocols Implementation

A layer can be built in software , in hardware , or both. The upper layers deal with data and programs, so they are software; the bottom layers deal with signals and timing, so they need hardware. The split: application, presentation, session and transport are software (part of the operating system and the applications). The network layer is mixed hardware and software (routers have special forwarding hardware, and hosts run IP in software). The data link and physical layers are in hardware , on the network interface card (NIC) : the card builds the frames, checks the MAC address and turns bits into signals. Which layers are implemented in hardware on the NIC? The network layer is implemented in a mix of hardware and software. The transport layer is implemented in: OSI Protocols Implementation A protocol layer can be implemented in software, in hardware, ■ or in a combination of the two Application, Presentation, Session and Transport are ■ implemented in software Network is a mixed implementation of hardware and software ■ Physical and data link are implemented in hardware in the ■ network interface card (NIC)
Peer-to-Peer Processes

Peers are the processes at the same layer on different machines; the communication between them is called peer-to-peer . In the figure, device A’s layer 4 is the peer of device B’s layer 4, even though their data actually travels down, across and up. Look at which layers the intermediate nodes have: only 1 to 3 . That means layers 4 to 7 talk end to end : A’s transport layer talks directly to B’s, and the routers in between never touch it. Layers 1 to 3 talk hop by hop : A talks to the first router, which talks to the next, and so on. This end-to-end vs. hop-by-hop split is one of the most tested ideas in the deck. Which layers communicate end to end, without the intermediate nodes taking part? Peers are: Peer-to-Peer Processes Peers are entities (processes, hardware devices) on two or more machines communicating at a given layer
OSI model-Basic Operation

Each layer talks to its peer using formatted blocks of data called Protocol Data Units (PDUs) . A PDU has two parts: the data (payload) handed down by the layer above, and the current layer’s own control information (requests and instructions for its peer). Every layer builds its own PDU, which is why each layer’s PDU has a different name (slide 51). The control information goes in a header in front of the data. The data link layer is the only exception : it adds a header and a trailer at the end. The trailer holds the error-detection code (such as a CRC), which is placed at the end so it can be calculated as the bits go out. A header is read and acted on only by the peer layer on the receiving node . The receiver’s transport layer reads the transport header; it never looks at the network header (the network layer already removed it). That rule is what keeps the layers independent. Only the data link layer adds a trailer (for error detection). Ch 3 Part 1, slide 4 : Framing adds the header and trailer Which layer adds both a header and a trailer? The header added by the transport layer is read by the receiver’s transport layer only. A PDU consists of: OSI model-Basic Operation Peer-to-Peer communication: Each layer on a sending ■ node communicates (logically) with its peer layer on the receiving node using formatted blocks of data called Protocol Data Units (PDU) PDU = combination of data (payload) from the next higher ■ layer and the control information of the current layer (Specific requests and instructions) Control information are given in the header fields of the ■ block except for the data link (has both header and trailer) Control information is read and executed ONLY by the peer ■ layer on the receiving node
An exchange using the OSI model (Figure 2.4)

Follow the data down the left side: the application’s data D7 gets header H7 , then the presentation layer adds H6 to that whole block, and so on down to the data link layer, which adds H2 and the trailer T2 . The physical layer sends the result as a stream of bits. On the right side the reverse happens: each layer removes its own header and passes the rest up, until the application gets D7 back. Note that each lower layer treats everything from above (headers included) as plain data. In the OSI exchange figure, which headers does the data link layer treat as plain data? Figure 2.4 An exchange using the OSI model
Data Encapsulation

Encapsulation means a layer puts the entire PDU from the layer above inside its own data field, without looking inside or changing it . The network layer doesn’t know or care that there is a TCP header in its data; to it, it is just bytes to carry. Think of putting a sealed letter inside an envelope, then that envelope inside a courier bag: each wrapper adds its own label but never opens what is inside. As a formula: PDU of layer N-1 = PDU of layer N + control information of layer N-1 . For example, a packet (layer 3) = a segment (layer 4) + an IP header; a frame (layer 2) = a packet + an Ethernet header and trailer. Data encapsulation means that layer N-1: During encapsulation, a lower layer inspects and changes the upper layer’s header. A frame is equal to: Data Encapsulation Data encapsulation refers to the fact that layer N-1 carries in its data part the PDU of layer N without any knowledge of its content and its different parts.
Decapsulation

Decapsulation is encapsulation in reverse, at the receiver. Each layer reads its own header (and trailer at layer 2), acts on it, removes it, and passes the remaining data up. By the time the data reaches the application, every header added by the sender has been removed by its peer. What does each layer do during decapsulation?
How Hosts Talk over a Network

Slides 17 to 24 are one animation of a single message going from one host to another. Follow it slowly once: it is encapsulation and decapsulation in action, with real names (TCP, IP, Ethernet). It starts at the top: an application needs to send data. The application, presentation and session layers prepare it (format it, maybe encrypt or compress it, and keep track of the conversation). In TCP/IP all three are one application layer. In TCP/IP, which layer does the job of OSI’s application, presentation and session layers? How Hosts Talk over a Network

The transport layer (TCP here) adds the TCP header . The most important fields in it are the port numbers : the source port identifies the sending application, and the destination port identifies which application on the other host should get the data (for example 443 for a secure web server). Ch 9, slide 9 : Process-to-process delivery with ports What does the TCP header carry that identifies the receiving application? How Hosts Talk over a Network

The network layer adds the IP header , which carries the source and destination IP addresses : the address of the sending host and of the final destination host. These two addresses are what routers read to forward the packet across networks. The IP header added by the network layer contains: How Hosts Talk over a Network IP Header TCP Header DATA Application Application Presentation Presentation Session Session Transport Transport NNeettwwoorrkk Network Data Link Data Link Physical Physical Network layer builds packet with source and destination IP address. Passes to data link layer for transmission
How Hosts Talk over a Network

The data link layer wraps the packet in a frame , adding the Ethernet header (with source and destination MAC addresses ) and a trailer. The destination MAC is the next device on this link , not necessarily the final host. Then the physical layer turns the frame into bits and sends them as signals on the cable. The destination MAC address in the sender’s Ethernet frame is the address of: How Hosts Talk over a Network Ethernet IP Header TCP Header DATA Application Application Presentation Presentation Session Session Transport Transport Network Network DDaattaa LLiinnkk Data Link PPhhyyssiiccaall Physical Data Link layer frames up packet and forwards data. Uses MAC address as destination address.
How Hosts Talk over a Network

At the receiver, the physical layer turns the signals back into bits. The data link layer checks the destination MAC address: if it matches (or is a broadcast), it checks the trailer for errors, removes the frame header and trailer, and passes the packet up. If it doesn’t match, the frame is dropped right there. What does the receiving data link layer do if the destination MAC address is not its own (and not broadcast)? Uses MAC address as destination address.
How Hosts Talk over a Network

The network layer reads the IP header. Since the destination IP address is this host’s own, it knows the packet has arrived, removes the IP header, and passes the segment up to TCP (the IP header’s protocol field says it is TCP). How does the receiving network layer know the packet has reached its destination? How Hosts Talk over a Network IP Header TCP Header DATA Application Application Presentation Presentation Session Session Transport Transport Network NNeettwwoorrkk Data Link Data Link Physical Physical Network layer looks at destination address. See’s the address as its own. Passes packet to TCP.
How Hosts Talk over a Network

The transport layer reads the TCP header and uses the destination port number to decide which application process gets the data. That is how a computer running a browser, an email program and a game at once gives each its own data. Which address does the receiving transport layer use to choose the application? How Hosts Talk over a Network TCP Header DATA Application Application Presentation Presentation Session Session Transport TTrraannssppoorrtt Network Network Data Link Data Link Physical Physical TCP identifies which application to pass data to by destination port number.
How Hosts Talk over a Network

Finally the application receives exactly the data the sender’s application sent. On the wire, the order of headers from the front is Ethernet | IP | TCP | data (and the Ethernet trailer at the end), because the lowest layer’s header is added last, so it is outermost. On the wire, the order of headers in front of the data is: How Hosts Talk over a Network DATA Application AApppplliiccaattiioonn Presentation PPrreesseennttaattiioonn Session SSeessssiioonn Transport Transport Network Network Data Link Data Link Physical Physical Application processes data.
Physical Layer

From here the deck goes through each layer’s job, bottom to top. The physical layer moves individual bits from one node to the next node on the link (one hop). It doesn’t know what the bits mean, which frame they belong to, or where they are finally going; it only makes sure that a 1 sent is received as a 1. The physical layer is responsible for moving: Physical Layer The physical layer is responsible for movements of individual bits from one hop (node) to the next.
Physical Layer

The physical layer deals with the actual medium. It defines the physical characteristics of the interfaces and the media: how devices connect to each other and to the link (topology), the shape, size and number of pins of connectors, which voltages and currents are used, what type of medium (twisted pair, fibre, wireless), and the transmission mode (simplex, half- or full-duplex). It also decides how bits are represented : each bit is encoded into an electrical or optical signal (for example, one voltage for 1 and another for 0). It sets the data rate , the number of bits sent per second, also called the transmission rate. And it handles synchronisation of bits : the sender and receiver clocks must agree, so the receiver samples each bit at the right moment and doesn’t miss or double-count bits. Devices that work only at this layer: the repeater (regenerates a weak signal) and the hub. The network card also has a physical-layer part (the part that sends and receives signals). They don’t read addresses at all, they only handle signals. Ch 2 Part 1, slide 2 : The physical layer in depth Ch 6, slide 4 : Hubs and repeaters Which device operates only at the physical layer? Data rate (bits per second) is defined by the physical layer. Making sure the sender’s and receiver’s clocks agree so each bit is read at the right time is: The shape of a connector and the number of its pins are defined by which layer? Physical Layer Deals with the actual communication media ■ Defines the physical characteristics of interfaces ■ and transmission media the way devices are connected to each other and to the link ■ (topology) Shape, size and number of pins of connectors ■ What voltages and currents are used ■ The type of transmission media ■ Transmission mode (duplex type) ■ Representation of bits – encoding into Electrical or Optical signals ■ Data Rate = transmission rate = bandwidth (number of bits sent per ■ second) Synchronization of bits (sender and receiver clocks must be ■ synchronized) Devices that operates at this level: Network card, repeater ■
RJ-45 connector

This is a concrete example of a physical-layer specification: the RJ-45 connector used on Ethernet cables. The female socket is in the NIC or networking device, and the male plug is on the cable. Its shape, size and 8 pins are defined by the physical layer, so any Ethernet cable fits any Ethernet port. The RJ-45 connector is an example of something specified by which layer? In NIC or networking device Connected to the Cable
Data Link Layer

The data link layer’s PDU is the frame . Its job is node-to-node (hop-to-hop) delivery: moving a frame across one direct link from one node to the next node. It doesn’t plan the whole route; it only gets the frame safely across the current link. Two duties are on the slide. Framing : dividing the stream of bits into frames, so the receiver knows where each unit starts and ends. Physical addressing : putting the sender’s and receiver’s physical addresses in the frame header. The physical address has many names that all mean the same thing: MAC address , hardware address, NIC address, LAN address, local address. It is burned into the network card. The MAC address says which device on the current link should receive the frame. In A ── Router ── B, A’s frame carries the router’s MAC as destination, because the router is the next device on A’s link. The router then builds a new frame with B’s MAC for the next link. So the MAC addresses change at every hop. Destination MAC = the NEXT HOP, not the final host. Destination IP = the final host. The PDU of the data link layer is the: Host A sends to host B through one router. The destination MAC address in A’s frame is: Which is NOT another name for the physical address? Dividing the stream of bits into units the receiver can recognise is called: Data Link Layer Data Link layer PDU is called frame ■ Transfers frames across direct connections Node- ■ to-Node (hop-to-hop) delivery Framing: dividing the stream of bits into units called ■ frames Physical Addressing: sender and receiver ■ physical addresses (Local address – hardware address – NIC address – LAN address) Physical address = MAC address = ■ hardware/NIC address MAC tells us WHICH DEVICE should receive this ■ frame on the current link. A ───── Router ───── B Change Frame: Destination MAC = Router
Note: data link layer

Memorise this one-line definition word for word: the data link layer moves frames from one hop (node) to the next . Compare it with the physical layer (bits, hop to hop) and the network layer (packets, source to destination): the exam often gives you the definition and asks which layer it is. “Responsible for moving frames from one hop (node) to the next” defines which layer? Note The data link layer is responsible for moving frames (data link PDU) from one hop (node) to the next.
Data Link Layer

The figure shows the frame being built: the data link layer takes the packet from layer 3 and adds a header H2 in front and a trailer T2 at the end. It is the only layer that adds a trailer. Between the two data link layers, the logical unit is a frame; between the two physical layers, it is just bits. The data link layer is the only layer that adds a trailer. Data Link Layer frames Data Link Data Link Layer Layer bits Physical Physical Layer Layer
Node-to-node delivery (Figure 2.7)

The path from A to F goes through intermediate systems B and E. Each hop ( A to B , B to E , E to F ) is a separate data link delivery, possibly on a different kind of link (Ethernet on one, Wi-Fi or a WAN link on another). The data link layer on each hop knows nothing about the others. A frame travels A to B to E to F. How many separate data link deliveries are there? Figure 2.7 Node-to-node delivery
Example 1 (Figure 2.8)

Station 10 sends to station 87 on a bus , which is a shared link. The frame carries source physical address 10 and destination physical address 87 . Because it is a bus, every station receives the signal, but each one compares the destination address with its own: only 87 matches, so only 87 keeps the frame, and the others drop it. This is physical addressing at work on one link. On a bus LAN, station 10 sends a frame to station 87. Which stations receive it and which one keeps it? In Example 1, what are the source and destination addresses in the frame? Figure 2.8 Example 1
Network Layer

The network layer’s PDU is the packet , also called a datagram . Its job is source-to-destination (host-to-host) delivery: getting a packet from the original sender all the way to the final destination host, possibly across many networks . This is the difference from the data link layer, which only crosses one link. To do that it needs logical addressing : a globally unique address that identifies each host on the Internet, called the IP address . Unlike the MAC address, which is burned into the card and only matters on the local link, the IP address says where the host is in the network as a whole. Routing : the connecting devices ( routers ) decide the best path for each packet towards its destination and forward it. Each router looks at the destination IP address and picks the next hop. That is the core of Chapters 7 and 8. IP = end-to-end destination. MAC = next-hop destination. Ch 7, slide 3 : Network-layer duties in depth Host-to-host delivery across multiple networks is the job of the: The IP address changes at each hop, while the MAC address stays the same end to end. Which device uses the destination IP address to choose the best path? The network layer PDU is called a: Network Layer Network Layer PDU is called Packet or Datagram ■ Source-to-destination (host-to-host) delivery ■ of a PACKET possible across MULTIPLE networks. Logical addressing (Network address) ■ ▪ A unique global address that distinguishes each host connected to the Internet ▪ In the Internet it is called IP address ▪ Routing ▪ Network connecting devices (routers ) route or switch the packets to their final destination . through the best path ▪ IP address = end-to-end destination MAC address = next-hop destination
Note: network layer

The one-line definition to memorise: the network layer delivers individual packets from the source host to the destination host . Note “individual”: each packet is handled on its own, with no idea that it belongs to a larger message. Putting the message back together is the transport layer’s job. The network layer knows which message each packet belongs to and keeps them in order. Note The network layer is responsible for the delivery of individual packets from the source host to the destination host.
Network Layer

The network layer adds only a header ( H3 ), no trailer. The header carries the source and destination IP addresses. It is added at the source host and removed at the destination host; routers in between read it but keep it. What does the network layer add to the segment? Network Layer
Source-to-destination delivery (Figure 2.10)

This figure joins the last two ideas. The network layer sees one end-to-end delivery, A to F. Underneath, the data link layer makes it happen as a chain of hop-to-hop deliveries: A to B, B to E, E to F. One network-layer trip = several data-link trips. How do the network and data link layers divide the work of getting a packet from A to F? Figure 2.10 Source-to-destination delivery
Example 2 (Figure 2.11)

A packet goes from logical address A to P , crossing two routers. Look at which addresses change. The logical (IP) addresses A and P stay the same the whole way, because they identify the original sender and the final receiver. The physical (MAC) addresses are replaced on every link , because each frame only travels one hop: on the first link they are A’s and the first router’s, on the next link the two routers’, and on the last link the second router’s and P’s. This is the classic exam question for this deck. A packet travels from host A to host P across two routers. Which addresses change on the way and which stay the same? In Example 2, on the link between the two routers, what are the destination addresses? Figure 2.11 Example 2
Transport Layer

The transport layer is responsible for process-to-process delivery of the entire message . A host runs many programs (processes) at once; the network layer gets data to the right computer , and the transport layer gets it to the right program on that computer. The network layer treats every packet independently : it doesn’t know that packet 1 and packet 2 belong to the same message, so they may take different routes and arrive out of order. The transport layer makes sure the whole message arrives intact and in order : it splits the message into pieces, numbers them, and puts them back together at the receiver. The transport layer’s PDU is the segment . Its address is the port address (port number), which identifies a process: for example, port 80 for a web server, 25 for email. So, bottom-up: MAC finds the device on the link, IP finds the host, and the port finds the process. Ch 9, slide 3 : Transport-layer services Transport-layer addressing uses: The transport layer PDU is a: Packets of a message arrive out of order. Which layer puts them back in order? Transport Layer The transport layer is responsible for Process-to-Process ■ delivery of the ENTIRE MESSAGE The network layer handles end-to-end (source-to-destination) ■ delivery of INDIVIDUAL PACKETS; no relationship between packets, each one is considered independently but the transport layer ensures whole message arrives intact and in order Transport PDU is called SEGMENT ■ Process addressing ■ Port address ■
Note: transport layer

The one-line definition: the transport layer delivers a message from one process to another. If a question says “process to process” or mentions ports, the answer is transport. “Responsible for the delivery of a message from one process to another” defines: Note The transport layer is responsible for the delivery of a message from one process to another.
Reliable process-to-process delivery of a message (Figure 2.12)

The figure puts the two kinds of delivery side by side. The network layer is host to host : it gets the data from the source computer to the destination computer. The transport layer is process to process : a TCP segment from source port 52000 (a browser picked a temporary port) to destination port 443 (the web server’s HTTPS port). A segment goes from port 52000 to port 443. What kind of delivery is this? Figure 2.12 Reliable process-to-process delivery of a message
Transport layer (Figure 2.12)

At the sender, the transport layer splits a long message into segments , each with its own header H4 (with the port numbers and a sequence number). At the receiver, it uses the sequence numbers to reassemble them in order, even if the network delivered them out of order. What does the transport layer do to a long message at the sender? Figure 2.12 Transport layer
Addressing

TCP/IP uses three levels of address , one for each of three layers: the physical (MAC) address at the data link layer, the IP (logical) address at the network layer, and the port address at the transport layer. Each answers a different question: which device on this link, which host on the Internet, which process on that host. Which three addresses does TCP/IP use? Addressing Figure 2.16 Pg 35 FOROUZAN03
Layer Addresses

Learn the pairs: port address with transport , IP address with network , physical (MAC) address with data link . The physical layer has no address (it just sends bits), and the application layer uses names such as URLs or email addresses, which DNS turns into IP addresses (Chapter 10). Bottom-up: MAC (L2) → IP (L3) → Port (L4). Which address belongs to the data link layer? Which address identifies a process on a host? Layer Addresses
Session

The session layer sets up, manages and ends sessions (connections) between applications, and keeps each application’s data separate from the others. Examples on the slide: an FTP program downloading several files at once, several Telnet (remote login) connections from one host, or browsing many web pages at the same time. Each is its own session. Dialog control : the session layer decides who may send when. The two processes can talk in full-duplex (both at once) or half-duplex (taking turns). Synchronisation : the session layer inserts checkpoints into a long transmission. If the connection crashes, the transfer can continue from the last checkpoint instead of starting over. For example, if a 1,000-page transfer has a checkpoint every 100 pages and fails at page 523, only pages 501 onward are resent. Adding checkpoints so a long transfer can resume after a crash is done by the: Deciding whether two processes talk at the same time or take turns is called: A user browses several web pages at once, and each keeps its data separate. Which layer manages this? Session Setting up, managing, and terminating sessions ■ (connections) between different applications Keeping different applications data separate from other ■ application data Multiple file downloads requested by a particular FTP ■ application Multiple telnet (remote connection to a device) ■ connections from a single host Browsing many Web pages at the same time ■ Dialog control ■ Full/Half duplex: Processes either send and receive data ■ at the same time or at different times Synchronization checkpoints ■ Allow long transmissions to continue from where they ■ were after the connection crash
Session layer (Figure 2.12)

The “syn” marks in the figure are the synchronisation checkpoints from the previous slide. They are inserted into the data stream so that, after a failure, both sides know how far the transfer got. What are the “syn” marks in the session layer figure? Figure 2.12 Session layer
Presentation

The presentation layer is about how data looks (its syntax), not what it means. Its first job is translation : different computers may represent data differently. The sender’s layer converts its format into a common format , and the receiver’s layer converts the common format into its own. The slide’s example: typing “Cisco” on a mainframe using the EBCDIC code would show up as “¢1½3?” on a PC using ASCII unless it is translated. Its other two jobs are encryption/decryption (making data unreadable to outsiders and readable again at the receiver) and compression (fewer bits, which matters for multimedia such as video and audio). Presentation is about HOW data looks: translate, encrypt, compress. Encryption, compression and translation belong to the: “Cisco” typed on an EBCDIC mainframe shows as “¢1½3?” on an ASCII PC. Which presentation-layer job prevents this? Why is compression especially useful for multimedia? Presentation Translation ■ Allows devices with different data representations ■ to communicate (interoperability). Sender format 🡺 common format ■ 🡺 Receiver format The input of “Cisco” on a Mainframe terminal, ■ which is working with an EBCDIC code set, would result in “¢¹½³? “ on a PC, because it uses ASCII. Encryption/decryption ■ Compression => Less bits (multimedia applications) ■
Presentation layer (Figure 2.13)

The figure shows the presentation layer adding its own header H6 to the data from the application layer, and the peer presentation layer at the receiver removing it. Inside, the data may have been translated, encrypted or compressed. Which header does the presentation layer add? Figure 2.13 Presentation layer
Application

The application layer is the one users touch: it provides the user interface and the network services that let applications use the network. Examples on the slide: a web browser uses HTTP to access the World Wide Web, Telnet gives remote access to another host, FTP handles file transfer, access and management, and mail services (SMTP) deliver email. Ch 10, slide 3 : Application layer: DNS A web browser accesses the World Wide Web using which application-layer protocol? Remote access to another host is provided by: Application User interface and Network services ■ that allow user applications to access the network Internet Browser uses the HTTP ■ application-layer protocol to access a WWW Telnet => remote host access ■ File transfer, access and management ■ Mail services ■
Application layer (Figure 2.15)

The figure shows user applications such as SMTP (email), Telnet (remote login) and HTTP (web) sitting in the application layer. These are the programs whose messages travel down the stack. Which of these sits in the application layer? Figure 2.15 Application layer
TCP/IP Protocol Suite

TCP/IP was developed in the 1970s. It is a suite (a family) of protocols named after its two most important ones, TCP (transport) and IP (network), but it includes others such as UDP . The textbook version has five layers . The mapping to OSI: the bottom four TCP/IP layers (physical, data link, network, transport) match OSI’s bottom four. OSI’s top three layers (session, presentation, application) are combined into a single application layer in TCP/IP. So the session and presentation jobs (checkpoints, encryption, compression) are done inside applications when they are needed. The textbook TCP/IP model has 5 layers; the original TCP/IP model (slide 54) has 4. In TCP/IP, which OSI layers are merged into the application layer? The TCP/IP protocol suite in the textbook has five layers. TCP/IP is named after: TCP/IP Protocol Suite Developed in 1970s ■ ▪ Is a suite of protocols named after the two most important protocols TCP and IP but includes other protocols such as UDP, etc Consists of Five layers ■ The first four lower layers correspond to the first four ■ layers of the OSI model. The three top layers in the OSI model, however, ■ are represented in TCP/IP by a single layer called the application layer.
Layers in the TCP/IP protocol suite (Figure 1.17)

Each TCP/IP layer has its own PDU name: layer 5 application: message ; layer 4 transport: segment (or user datagram for UDP); layer 3 network: packet (datagram); layer 2 data link: frame ; layer 1 physical: bits . Exams ask “what is the PDU at layer 3?” or “at which layer is the PDU called a frame?”, so learn it in both directions. “My Silly Pet Fish Bites”: Message, Segment, Packet, Frame, Bits. The PDU at layer 3 is called a: Which PDU belongs to the transport layer? At which layer is the unit of data simply bits? Figure 1.17 Layers in the TCP/IP protocol suite Message Segment Packet Frame Bits 51
TCP/IP and OSI model

The same mapping as slide 50, drawn side by side: OSI application, presentation and session become TCP/IP’s application layer, and the bottom four line up one-to-one. The bottom four layers of TCP/IP correspond one-to-one with the bottom four layers of OSI. Figure 2.12: TCP/IP and OSI model
TCP/IP and OSI model: protocols

Know which protocols live in which layer. Application : SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer), HTTP (web), DNS (names to IP addresses), SNMP (network management), Telnet (remote login). Transport : TCP , UDP and SCTP. Network : IP , with its helpers ICMP (error messages, used by ping), IGMP (multicast groups), ARP (IP address to MAC address) and RARP. Below that are the underlying physical networks (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). A common trap is placing ARP or ICMP in the transport layer. Which protocol belongs to the transport layer? ARP and ICMP sit in which TCP/IP layer? DNS belongs to which layer? Figure 2.16 TCP/IP and OSI model
Original TCP/IP Model (4-layers)

The original TCP/IP model has only four layers: application , transport , internet (= network) and network access (= data link + physical combined). The textbook’s five-layer version simply splits network access into two. If an exam says TCP/IP has four layers, it means this original model; five layers means the textbook version. In the original 4-layer TCP/IP model, the network access layer corresponds to: What is the “internet” layer of the original TCP/IP model? Original TCP/IP Model (4-layers)

n: Physical Layer

The deck goes from what a signal is, to the two kinds (analog and digital) and how to measure them (frequency and period for analog, bit rate and bit interval for digital), to what goes wrong on the way (attenuation, distortion, noise), to how long delivery takes (propagation, transmission, queuing, latency), and finishes with the bandwidth-delay product and wavelength. This is the calculation deck, and Tutorial 3 is mostly calculations from it. Most marks are lost on units, not formulas: write the formula, convert everything to base units first (seconds, hertz, bits, metres, bits per second), then calculate, then convert the answer to the unit asked. Remember 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 ms = 10⁻³ s, 1 µs = 10⁻⁶ s, and k = 10³, M = 10⁶, G = 10⁹. Formula sheet: f = 1/T · bit interval = 1/bit rate · propagation = distance / speed · transmission = size in bits / bandwidth · BDP = bandwidth × delay · wavelength = speed / f. A message is 2 KB. How many bits is that, using 1 KB = 1000 bytes? Chapter 02 Physical Layer Data Communications ◼ and Networking, With TCP/IP protocol suite Sixth Edition Behrouz A.
