Chapter 2: Outline

Chapter 2 has six sections. This part covers 2.1 signals and 2.2 signal impairment , plus the delay definitions (propagation, transmission, latency) and the bandwidth-delay product. Part 2 covers digital and analog transmission, multiplexing (Tutorial 3 asks a scenario on it) and transmission media . Related question: Q3 · multiplexing several departments onto one link You are setting up a network for a large office. Data from different departments must be sent over a single high-capacity link to the internet. Which physical layer concept from the slides would you apply here? Chapter 2: Outline 2.1 SIGNALS ◼ 2.2 SIGNAL IMPAIRMENT ◼ 2.3 DIGITAL TRANSMISSION ◼ 2.4 ANALOG TRANSMISSION ◼ 2.5 MULTIPLEXING ◼ 2.6 TRANSMISSION MEDIA ◼ 2
Physical Layer

The physical layer defines the physical characteristics of the interfaces and the media: how devices are connected to each other and to the link (topology), the shape, size and number of pins on connectors, the voltages and currents, the type of medium (copper, fibre, wireless) and the transmission mode (simplex, half- or full-duplex). You saw this list in Chapter 1 Part 2; this chapter goes into detail. Three more duties. Representation of bits : bits are encoded into electrical or optical signals. Data rate (transmission rate, also called bandwidth in this course): how many bits are sent per second. Synchronisation of bits : the sender’s and receiver’s clocks must match, so the receiver reads each bit at the right instant. Devices that work at this layer: the network card (its signalling part), the hub and the repeater . They handle signals only; they never read an address. Ch 1 Part 2, slide 26 : First look at the physical layer Which of these is NOT a physical layer duty? Which device works at the physical layer? Physical Layer Deals with the actual communication media ◼ Defines the physical characteristics of interfaces ◼ and transmission media the way devices are connected to each other and to the link ◼ (topology) Shape, size and number of pins of connectors ◼ What voltages and currents are used ◼ The type of transmission media ◼ Transmission mode (duplex type) ◼ Representation of bits – encoding into Electrical or Optical ◼ signals Data Rate = transmission rate = bandwidth (number of bits ◼ sent per second) Synchronization of bits (sender and receiver clocks must be ◼ synchronized) Devices that operates at this level: Network card, hub, ◼ repeater
Signals: data must become electromagnetic signals

A cable can’t carry the number 1 or the letter A. Data has to be turned into a signal , a form of electromagnetic energy that can travel through the medium: a changing voltage on copper wire, pulses of light in a fibre-optic cable, or radio waves through the air. The left picture is an electrical signal on copper; the right one is light pulses in fibre. Turning data into a suitable signal, and back again at the receiver, is the physical layer’s core job. To be transmitted, data must be transformed to electromagnetic signals. In a fibre-optic cable, data travels as: Signals Note To be transmitted, data must be transformed to electromagnetic signals. Light Pulses Over Fiber-Optic Cable Electrical Signals Over Copper Cable
A Transmission System

Transmission is communicating data by sending signals through a channel. A signal is electromagnetic energy that moves through the medium and carries information. The basic system has three parts: a transmitter , a communication channel and a receiver . The transmitter turns information into a signal suited to the medium and injects energy into the channel: a telephone turns your voice into electric current, a NIC turns bits into electric current or light pulses. The receiver takes the energy from the medium and turns it back into a usable form: the phone turns current back into sound, the NIC turns current or light back into bits. A NIC is both a transmitter and a receiver. What is a signal? When a NIC receives light pulses and turns them into bits, it is acting as: A Transmission System Transmitter Receiver Communication channel Transmission: Communication of data by propagation and processing of signals through a communication channel Signal: Electromagnetic energy that moves through the transmission medium and carries some information. Transmitter Converts information into signal suitable for transmission ◼ Injects energy into communications medium or channel ◼ Telephone converts voice into electric current ◼ NIC converts bits into electric current or pulses of light ◼ Receiver Receives energy from medium ◼ Converts received signal into form suitable for delivery to user ◼ Telephone converts current into voice ◼ NIC converts electric current or pulses of light into bits ◼
Analog and Digital

Analog data is continuous : it can take any value in a range, like the exact loudness of a sound or the temperature. Digital data is discrete : it takes separate values, like text characters or whole numbers. The same split applies to signals. An analog signal is a smoothly varying wave that can have an infinite number of values in a range over time. A digital signal is a series of voltage pulses (a square wave) with only a limited number of values : it stays at one constant level, then jumps to another. Separately, a signal can be periodic , meaning it repeats the same pattern over identical time periods called cycles , or aperiodic , meaning it changes without a repeating pattern . These are two different classifications: analog/digital is about which values the signal can take, periodic/aperiodic is about whether its pattern repeats over time. So a signal can be periodic analog, aperiodic digital, and so on. Analog/digital is about the VALUES; periodic/aperiodic is about the PATTERN over time. They are separate classifications. A signal that can have an infinite number of values in a range is: A periodic signal repeats its pattern over identical periods called cycles. Text and integers are examples of: Whether a signal is analog or digital, and whether it is periodic or aperiodic, are two separate classifications. Analog and Digital Analog Data ◼ : Continuous value data (sound, light, temperature) Digital Data: ◼ Discrete value (text, integers, symbols) Analog Signals ◼ : Continuously varying electromagnetic wave have an infinite number of values over a period of time ◼ Digital Signals ◼ : Series of voltage pulses (square wave) have only a limited number of values over a period of time. ◼ Maintains a constant level then changes to another constant level ◼ Signals are classified into: ◼ Periodic Signals ◼ : Consists of repeated patterns over identical period of times (cycles) Aperiodic Signals ◼ : change without a pattern that repeats over time
Comparison of analog and digital signals (Figure 2.2)

Picture (a) is analog: a smooth wave that passes through every value between its highs and lows. Picture (b) is digital: flat steps that jump between a few levels. The rule to remember from the next slide: in data communication we commonly use periodic analog signals (a repeating sine wave, used as a carrier, for example in radio) and aperiodic digital signals (the bit stream of real data doesn’t repeat, because the data itself doesn’t). In data communication we commonly use: Figure 2.2 Comparison of analog and digital signals In data communication, we commonly use periodic analog signals and aperiodic digital signals. 7
Note: periodic analog, aperiodic digital

The slide repeats the rule on purpose because it is a classic MCQ: periodic analog and aperiodic digital . Why aperiodic digital? Because a digital signal carries real data such as 10110010…, which doesn’t repeat in a regular pattern. Why periodic analog? Because a pure repeating sine wave is easy to generate and can be changed (modulated) to carry information. Why are digital signals in data communication usually aperiodic? Note: In data communication, we commonly use periodic analog signals and aperiodic digital signals.
Note: frequency

Frequency is how fast a signal changes over time: the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz) . If the signal changes a lot in a short time, the frequency is high . If the signal changes slowly, over a long time, the frequency is low . Two extremes: a signal that never changes at all has a frequency of zero , and a signal that jumps instantly from one level to another has (in theory) an infinite frequency. A signal changes a lot in a very short time. Its frequency is: A signal that never changes has a frequency of zero. Note Frequency is the rate of change with respect to time. Change in a short span of time means high frequency. _/‾\_/‾\_/‾\_/‾\_ Change over a long span of time means low frequency. ____/‾‾‾\____/‾‾‾\____
Note: frequency and period

Frequency and period are inverses : f = 1/T and T = 1/f . The period T is the time one cycle takes, in seconds; the frequency f is the number of cycles per second, in hertz. If one cycle takes 0.5 s, then 2 cycles fit into a second, so f = 2 Hz. Tutorial 3, Question 5 asks exactly this: f = 5 kHz = 5,000 Hz, so T = 1/5,000 = 0.0002 s = 200 µs. Units pair up: s ↔ Hz, ms ↔ kHz, µs ↔ MHz, ns ↔ GHz. Q5 · period of a 5 kHz signal An analog signal has a frequency of 5 kHz. Explain what its period is and how frequency and period are mathematically related. An analog signal has a frequency of 2 kHz. Its period is: Period is measured in seconds. Frequency is measured in: Note Frequency and period are the inverse of each other.
Example

Worked example: home power is 60 Hz , so T = 1/60 = 0.0166 s. To convert seconds to milliseconds, multiply by 1000: 0.0166 × 1000 = 16.6 ms . So one cycle of mains power lasts about 16.6 ms. (In Saudi Arabia the mains frequency is also 60 Hz.) A signal has a frequency of 50 Hz. Its period is: Example The power we use at home has a frequency of 60 Hz. The period of this sine wave can be determined as follows: 1 second = 1000 ms
Example

Going the other way: the period is 100 ms , and the question wants kHz. Step 1, convert to base units: 100 ms = 0.1 s. Step 2, use the formula: f = 1/0.1 = 10 Hz . Step 3, convert to the unit asked: 10 Hz = 10/1000 = 0.01 kHz . Always do these three steps in that order, because dividing 1 by 100 (forgetting to convert ms) gives an answer 1000 times too small. A signal has a period of 4 ms. Its frequency is: What is the first step when a period is given in ms and the frequency is wanted in kHz? Example The period of a signal is 100 ms. What is its frequency in kilohertz?
Simple and composite signals

A simple signal is a single sine wave , so it has exactly one frequency : every cycle is identical and takes the same time. A composite signal is made of several sine waves with different frequencies (and possibly different amplitudes and phases) added together, so its cycles don’t all look the same. Real signals, such as voice or a digital bit stream, are composite. This is Tutorial 3, Question 8. Q8 · simple vs. composite signal What is the key difference between a simple signal and a composite signal, as described in the slides? A signal made of several sine waves with different frequencies is: Signals that have just one frequency are called simple signals, for example, the sine signal is simple signal (each cycle takes the same time) Signals that are composed of multiple frequencies are called composite signals (each cycle takes different time)
Digital Signals

A digital signal represents bits as voltage levels: here 1 = a positive voltage and 0 = zero voltage . Most digital signals are aperiodic , because the data they carry doesn’t repeat, so frequency and period don’t describe them well. Instead we use bit rate (bits per second) and bit interval (the time one bit takes), defined on slide 16. Why are frequency and period not used to describe most digital signals? Digital Signals 1 = Positive voltage > 0 0 = Zero voltage Most Digital Signals are Aperiodic ➔ Frequency is not appropriate
Two digital signals, one with two and one with four bit-levels

A digital signal can use more than two levels. With 2 levels , each level carries 1 bit (low = 0, high = 1), so 8 levels sent in one second carry 8 bits: 8 bps. With 4 levels , each level carries 2 bits (00, 01, 10, 11), so 8 levels in a second carry 16 bits: 16 bps. The rule: with L levels, each level carries log₂L bits . 8 levels carry 3 bits, 16 levels carry 4. More levels means more bits per second without changing how fast the signal changes level. A digital signal has 8 levels. How many bits does each level carry? A signal with 2 levels sends 8 levels per second (8 bps). A 4-level signal changing level just as fast sends: Two digital signals, one with two and one with four bit-levels ◼ Access the text alternative for slide images. 15
Bit rate and bit interval

Two measures for digital signals. The bit interval is the time needed to send one bit , the digital version of the period. The bit rate is the number of bits sent per second (bps), the digital version of frequency. It is also called digital bandwidth, transmission speed or link capacity. They are inverses: bit rate = 1/bit interval . Tutorial 3, Question 1: bit interval = 50 µs = 0.00005 s, so bit rate = 1/0.00005 = 20,000 bps = 20 Kbps . Q1 · bit rate from a 50 µs bit interval A digital signal has a bit interval of 0.00005 seconds (50 µs). What is the bit rate (bandwidth) of this signal in Kbps? A digital signal has a bit interval of 25 µs. Its bit rate is: The time needed to send one bit is the: Figure Bit rate and bit interval Bit Interval (digital signal period): The time required to send (represent) one single bit (time units) Bit Rate (digital bandwidth) = Transmission speed = Link Capacity: Number of bits sent per second (bps)
Example: bit interval

Worked example: bit rate = 2000 bps, so bit interval = 1/2000 = 0.0005 s. To convert seconds to microseconds, multiply by 10⁶: 0.0005 × 10⁶ = 500 µs . Sanity check: if each bit lasts half a millisecond, 2000 of them fill one second. A signal has a bit rate of 4000 bps. Each bit lasts: Example A digital signal has a bit rate of 2000 bps. What is the duration of each bit (bit interval) Solution The bit interval is the inverse of the bit rate. Bit interval = 1/ 2000 s = 0.000500 s = 0.000500 x 106 s = 500 s (microsecond)
Advantages of Digital Transmission

Why digital transmission is preferred: it is cheaper (digital chips are inexpensive), it can travel longer distances because repeaters regenerate a clean copy of the bits instead of boosting noise, it supports security and privacy through encryption , noise can be removed because the receiver only has to decide between a few levels, many signals can be combined by digital multiplexing , and both analog and digital data can be processed the same way once they are digital. Related question: Q2 · what a repeater does The slides mention that a “repeater” is a physical layer device. What is its primary function, and why is it necessary in digital transmission? Why can digital transmission cover longer distances? Advantages of Digital Transmission
Signal corruption

No medium is perfect. Each one passes some frequencies well, blocks others and weakens others. Because a real signal is composite (made of many frequencies), the medium treats its parts differently, so the signal that comes out is never exactly the signal that went in. The figure shows a sharp square wave coming out rounded. This is the reason impairments exist. Why does a signal come out of a medium different from how it went in? Signal corruption ▪ No transmission medium can pass all the signal frequencies safely ▪A medium may ▪ Pass some frequencies ▪ Block others ▪ Weaken others
Transmission Impairments

Impairments are the factors that make the received signal different from the transmitted one . There are three: attenuation (the signal gets weaker), distortion (the signal changes shape) and noise (unwanted signals get added). Learning what each one changes (strength, shape, or extra energy) is enough to identify it in any scenario. “ADN”: Attenuation (weaker), Distortion (reshaped), Noise (extra signal). Which is NOT a transmission impairment? Impairments are defined as factors that: Transmission Impairments Impairments: Factors that make the received signal different from the transmitted one
Attenuation

Attenuation is a loss of energy . As the signal travels, the medium resists it, and some of the energy is turned into heat (the slide’s example: a wire carrying a signal gets warm). So the signal gets weaker with distance . It also increases with frequency : higher-frequency signals lose strength faster, which is one reason high-speed links need shorter cables or better media. The fix depends on the signal. Amplifiers are used for analog signals: they boost the signal, but they also boost any noise in it. Repeaters are used for digital signals: they read the weak signal, work out which bits it carried, and regenerate a clean new copy. Tutorial 3, Question 2 asks what a repeater does and why it is needed: it regenerates a weakened or distorted digital signal so the data can travel farther without losing its form. Amplifiers boost noise too; repeaters regenerate the original bits. Q2 · repeater regenerates the weakened signal Loss of signal energy due to the resistance of the medium is called: What does a repeater do and why is it needed in digital transmission? Attenuation increases as the signal frequency increases. Which device handles attenuation for analog signals? Attenuation ▪ Attenuation: Loss of energy due to resisting the medium (Signal strength falls off with distance) ▪ Increases with signal frequency ▪ Ex. A wire carrying electrical signal becomes warm after some time ▪ Amplifiers (analog signals) and repeaters (digital signals) are used to handle attenuation ▪
Distortion

Distortion means the signal changes shape . It happens to composite signals because each frequency component travels through the medium at a slightly different speed, so the components arrive at slightly different times and no longer add up to the original shape. The slide’s example is a video call with distorted images or audio. The key word in a question is “shape”: weaker is attenuation, reshaped is distortion. A composite signal arrives with a changed shape. This impairment is: Why does distortion happen? Distortion ▪ Distortion : Signal changes in shape ▪ Example: In a video call, distorted images or audio delays may result from signal distortion during transmission. ▪
Noise

Noise is unwanted energy that gets added to the signal. Thermal noise comes from the random motion of electrons in the wire, which creates an extra signal that was never sent; it is always present. Induced noise comes from outside sources such as motors and electrical equipment (like a microwave or a large machine), which act as antennas sending interference into the cable. Tutorial 3, Question 9 is this case: errors caused by nearby electrical equipment are induced noise. Crosstalk is the effect of one wire on another: two wires lying beside each other, and one picks up the signal of the other. It is like hearing another conversation in the background of your phone call (Tutorial 3, Question 6). Twisting the wire pairs, as in twisted-pair cable, reduces it. Impulse noise is irregular, short spikes with high amplitude , caused by power lines or lightning . It is very critical for digital signals , and it is the primary source of errors in digital data communication, because a single spike can flip a whole run of bits. Crosstalk = “cross talk”: someone else’s conversation crossing into yours. Q6 · background conversation = crosstalk Q9 · nearby electrical equipment = induced noise You are on a phone call and hear a faint conversation in the background from another call. What type of signal impairment is this, and under which broader category does it fall? You are designing a system to transmit digital data over a long distance. It has significant errors because of electrical equipment nearby. Which impairment is the primary source, and how might you reduce it? Which noise is the primary source of error in digital data communication? Noise caused by the random motion of electrons in a wire is: Noise ▪ Thermal Noise due to random motion of electrons in a wire which will create an extra signal ▪ Induced Noise: caused by motors and electrical equipments. ▪ crosstalk noise : Two wires beside each others (hearing another conversation in the background while talking with the phone) ▪ Impulse noise: irregular pulses or noise spikes of short duration and high amplitude ▪ caused by power lines or lightning ▪ Very critical in case of digital signals (primary source of error in digital data communication)
Performance: propagation time and speed

Propagation time is the time one bit needs to travel from one node to the other: propagation time = distance / propagation speed . It depends only on how far the bit goes and how fast signals move in the medium. It does not depend on the size of the message or the bandwidth. The propagation speed is the speed of light in the medium: 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, a little less in air, and much less in a cable, about 2/3 of that, so roughly 2 × 10⁸ m/s . Tutorial 3, Question 4: 2,000 km = 2,000,000 m, so 2,000,000 / (2 × 10⁸) = 0.01 s = 10 ms . Always convert km to m before dividing by m/s. Convert km to m before dividing by m/s. Q4 · 2,000 km at 2 × 10⁸ m/s A sender and receiver are 2,000 km apart. The signal propagates at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the propagation time for a single bit? Two nodes are 4,000 km apart and the signal travels at 2 × 10⁸ m/s. The propagation time is: Doubling the size of a message doubles its propagation time. Propagation time = distance of the link (between the ◼ two nodes) / Propagation speed Propagation speed: Speed of light in the ◼ medium. Depends on the medium ◼ Light travels at 3x108 m/s Vacuum (free space), ◼ lower in the air and much lower in a cable (2/3 in vacuum)
Propagation Time

The figure defines propagation time visually: the bit leaves the sender at time t1, travels distance d, and arrives at time t2. Propagation time = t2 - t1 = d / propagation speed. A bit leaves at t1 and arrives at t2. The propagation time is: Propagation Time
Other Physical layer definitions – Transmission Time

Transmission time is the time the sender needs to push all the bits of a frame onto the link , from the NIC into the medium: transmission time = message size in bits / bandwidth (bps) . It depends on how big the message is and how fast the link is, not on distance. Tutorial 3, Question 7: 1 MB = 8 Mb (multiply bytes by 8), and 8 Mb / 1 Mbps = 8 s . Queuing time is the time each intermediate device (router, switch) holds the message in a queue before it can process and forward it. It depends on how busy the device is, so it changes all the time. Latency (delay) is the total time to deliver a message = transmission time + propagation time + processing time + queuing time . A simple way to remember what each term depends on: propagation = how far , transmission = how big , queuing = how busy , processing = how much work each device does. Propagation = how FAR. Transmission = how BIG. Queuing = how BUSY. 1 MB = 8 Mb: multiply bytes by 8 first. Q7 · 1 MB over 1 Mbps A network has a bandwidth of 1 Mbps. You need to send a 1-megabyte (MB) file. Ignoring propagation delay, what is the transmission time? A 2 MB file is sent over a 4 Mbps link (ignore propagation). Transmission time? Which delay depends on the size of the message? List the four components of latency. A router holds a packet while it waits for other packets to be forwarded first. Latency (delay): Total message delivery time = Transmission time + ◼ Propagation time + processing time+ queuing time
Example

Before calculating, guess which delay will dominate: the message is small (2.5 KB) and the link is very fast (1 Gbps), but the distance is huge (12,000 km). Small message on a fast link means a tiny transmission time; long distance means a noticeable propagation time. The next slide confirms it. A small message is sent over a very fast link across 12,000 km. Before calculating, which delay should you expect to dominate? Example What are the propagation time and the transmission time for a 2.5-kbyte message (an e-mail) if the bandwidth of the network is 1 Gbps? Assume that the distance between the sender and the receiver is 12,000 km and that light travels at 2.4 × 108 m/s. Solution We can calculate the propagation and transmission time as shown on the next slide:
Example (continued)

Propagation time = 12,000 km = 12,000 × 1000 m = 1.2 × 10⁷ m, divided by 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s = 0.05 s = 50 ms . Transmission time = 2.5 KB = 2500 × 8 = 20,000 bits, divided by 10⁹ bps = 0.00002 s = 0.020 ms . Propagation is 2,500 times bigger, so for a short message on a high-bandwidth link, propagation dominates and transmission can be ignored. For a short e-mail on a 1 Gbps link across 12,000 km, the transmission time dominates. What is the transmission time of a 2.5 KB message on a 1 Gbps link? The transmission time can be ignored.
Example

Same distance and speed as before, but now a large message (5 MB) on a slow link (1 Mbps). The propagation time will be the same 50 ms, because distance hasn’t changed. Guess before you look: a big message on a slow link should take a long time to push onto the wire. In the 5 MB example, what is the propagation time over 12,000 km at 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s? Example What are the propagation time and the transmission time for a 5-Mbyte message (an image) if the bandwidth of the network is 1 Mbps? Assume that the distance between the sender and the receiver is 12,000 km and that light travels at 2.4 × 108 m/s. Solution We can calculate the propagation and transmission times as shown on the next slide.
Example (continued)

Propagation is unchanged: 50 ms . Transmission = 5 MB = 5,000,000 × 8 = 40,000,000 bits, divided by 10⁶ bps = 40 s . Now transmission is 800 times bigger, so for a long message on a low-bandwidth link, transmission dominates and propagation can be ignored. Comparing slides 28 and 30 is the point: which delay matters depends on message size and bandwidth, not only on distance. A 5 MB image is sent on a 1 Mbps link over 12,000 km (2.4 × 10⁸ m/s). Which delay dominates? Compare the two examples (2.5 KB on 1 Gbps, and 5 MB on 1 Mbps, both over 12,000 km). What do they show? The propagation time can be ignored.
Example: a satellite link

A satellite link: A sends up to a satellite 36,000 km above, and the satellite sends down to B, another 36,000 km. So the total distance from A to B is 72,000 km = 7.2 × 10⁷ m. Propagation time = 7.2 × 10⁷ / (3 × 10⁸) = 0.24 s (each leg alone is 0.12 s). Signals in space travel at the vacuum speed of light, 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Transmission time = 2000 bytes = 16,000 bits, divided by 10⁹ bps = 0.000016 s = 16 µs . Propagation (240,000 µs) is 15,000 times larger. This is why satellite links feel slow for interactive use, like calls and games, even when their bandwidth is high: the delay comes from distance, and more bandwidth can’t reduce it. In the satellite example (36,000 km up, 36,000 km down, 3 × 10⁸ m/s), the propagation time from A to B is: In the satellite example, the transmission time of a 2000-byte frame at 1 Gbps is: Increasing the bandwidth of a satellite link reduces its propagation time. Propagation time=Distance/Propagation speed​ Transmission time=Message size in bits/Bandwidth​
Bandwidth-delay product (Figure 2.7)

Think of the link as a pipe . Its cross-section (how wide it is) is the bandwidth : how many bits can enter per second. Its length is the delay : how long a bit takes to get from one end to the other. Its volume , bandwidth × delay, is the bandwidth-delay product : the number of bits that fit inside the link at once, before the first one arrives. Tutorial 3, Question 10: 5 bps × 5 s = 25 bits . A 10 Mbps link with a 2 ms delay holds 10⁷ × 0.002 = 20,000 bits. This matters later because a sender should keep that many bits in flight to use the link fully. Q10 · 5 bps × 5 s A link has a bandwidth of 5 bps and a delay of 5 seconds. (a) What is its bandwidth-delay product? (b) If a sender transmits for 5 seconds, how many bits are “in the pipe”? A 10 Mbps link has a 2 ms delay. How many bits fill the link? In the pipe picture, what does the cross-section represent? Figure 2.7 Bandwidth-delay product We can think about the link between two points as a pipe. The cross section of the pipe represents the bandwidth, and the length of the pipe represents the delay. We can say the volume of the pipe defines the bandwidth-delay product bandwidth-delay product = Length of the link in bits 32
Filling the link with bits for case 1

Case 1: bandwidth 1 bps, delay 5 s. The sender puts one bit on the link each second, and each bit takes 5 s to arrive. When the first bit reaches the receiver, the sender has sent 5 bits, so 5 bits are in the link: 1 × 5 = 5. Bandwidth 1 bps, delay 5 s. How many bits are in the link when the first bit arrives? Figure Filling the link with bits for case 1
Filling the link with bits in case 2

Case 2: bandwidth 5 bps, same 5 s delay. Now 5 bits enter every second, so after 5 s the link holds 25 bits : 5 × 5 = 25. These are the Tutorial 3 numbers. Comparing the two cases: the same pipe length, but five times wider, holds five times more bits. Other Physical layer definitions - Wavelength

Wavelength is the distance a simple signal travels in one period , or the distance one cycle occupies in the medium. It depends on the frequency and on the medium (through its propagation speed): wavelength = propagation speed × period = propagation speed / frequency . Example: a 1 MHz signal at 2 × 10⁸ m/s has a wavelength of 2 × 10⁸ / 10⁶ = 200 m . Higher frequency means shorter wavelength. A 1 MHz signal travels at 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Its wavelength is: Wavelength depends on: If the frequency of a signal doubles in the same medium, its wavelength halves. Other Physical layer definitions - Wavelength Wavelength: ◼ the distance a simple signal can travel in one period (or the distance occupied by one cycle) Depends on both the signal frequency and the medium ◼ Wavelength = Propagation speed x Period ◼ = Propagation speed / frequency

n: Physical Layer

Transmission media come in two families. Guided (wired) media keep the signal inside a physical path: twisted pair , coaxial cable and fibre-optic cable . Unguided (wireless) media send the signal through the air: radio waves , microwaves and infrared . Exam questions on this deck are mostly “which medium fits this situation?” scenarios. For each medium, know what it is made of, one or two advantages, one or two disadvantages, and a typical use; for the wireless ones, also know the frequency range, whether it is omnidirectional or line-of-sight, and whether it passes through walls. Transmission medium and the physical layer

The transmission medium (or channel) is the physical path between the transmitter and the receiver: a cable or the air. It sits below the physical layer (some books call it layer 0) and is controlled by the physical layer, which decides what signals to put on it. So the medium itself isn’t a layer; it is what the bottom layer uses. Ch 1 Part 1, slide 3 : The medium as a component of data communication The transmission medium is located above the physical layer. The transmission medium is: Figure 7.1 Transmission medium and physical layer ▪Transmission medium(channel): the physical path between the transmitter and the receiver. ▪Located below the physical layer ▪Controlled by the physical layer
Classes of transmission media

Guided media guide the signal along a physical conductor, so it goes only where the cable goes: twisted pair and coaxial (both copper, carrying electrical signals) and fibre-optic (glass or plastic, carrying light). Unguided media have no physical conductor: the signal spreads through the air (or space) and any device with a suitable receiver can pick it up. The three types are radio waves , microwaves and infrared , listed from lowest to highest frequency. Guided = the signal is GUIDED along a physical path. Unguided = it just spreads through the air. Which is an unguided medium? Fibre-optic cable is classified as: Figure 7.2: Classes of transmission media 7.3
Guided media

The three guided media, from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest: twisted pair (used in nearly every office LAN), coaxial cable (cable TV, old Ethernet), and fibre-optic (backbones, long distances, high speed). Which guided medium is the most expensive but offers the highest speed? 7.1 Guided Media Twisted-Pair Cable Coaxial Cable Fiber-Optic Cable
Twisted pairs

A typical Ethernet cable holds four twisted pairs inside one plastic jacket, each pair with its own colour code (orange, green, blue, brown, each paired with a white-striped wire). The colours let installers wire both ends the same way. How many twisted pairs does a typical Ethernet cable contain? Twisted pairs
Twisted-pair cable

A twisted pair is two insulated copper wires twisted around each other in a regular spiral. The two wires together form one communication link : one carries the signal and the other is the reference, and the receiver looks at the difference between them. Why twist them? To reduce electrical interference (noise and crosstalk) from other pairs close by and from outside sources. Twisting makes both wires pick up the same interference, which then cancels out at the receiver (slide 8 shows how). The tighter the twisting, the better the cancellation, so more twists per length means better quality . Twisted pair is used in the telephone network between a house and the local exchange (the subscriber loop) and in LANs , where it is the standard Ethernet cable. Why are the wires in a twisted pair twisted? More twists per length gives better quality twisted-pair cable. Where is twisted pair used? Figure 7.3 Twisted-pair cable A twisted pair consists of: two ▪ insulated copper wires in a regular spiral pattern ▪A wire pair acts as a single communication link ▪Twisted to reduce electrical interference from similar pairs close by (more twists means better quality) ▪Used in: ▪Telephone network Between house and local exchange (subscriber loop) ▪LAN
Twist length: Category 3 vs. Category 5 UTP

The figure shows the difference twist length makes. Category 3 UTP has long twists, every 7.5 to 10 cm. Category 5 UTP is twisted much more tightly, every 0.6 to 0.85 cm. Because Cat 5 cancels interference better, it can carry higher frequencies and so higher data rates with less crosstalk. This is the practical meaning of “more twists = better quality”. Why can Category 5 UTP carry higher data rates than Category 3? Twist length of 7.5 cm to 10 cm Twist length 0.6 cm to 0.85 cm
Why twisting cancels interference

(a) With two parallel wires , one wire is always closer to the noise source, so it picks up more noise than the other. The receiver reads the difference between the wires, and an unequal amount of noise leaves a leftover (+6 in the figure) that corrupts the signal. (b) With a twisted pair , the two wires keep swapping positions along the cable, so over its length both pick up the same total noise . When the receiver subtracts one from the other, the noise cancels (a difference of 0), and only the real signal remains. Explain how twisting a pair of wires reduces noise. A twisted-pair receiver reads: B) The interference affects both wires equally overall, so the unwanted radiation is largely canceled.
UTP and STP cables

UTP is Unshielded Twisted Pair: the pairs sit directly inside a plastic cover. STP is Shielded Twisted Pair: the pairs are wrapped in a metal shield (foil or braided mesh) inside the plastic cover. The shield blocks outside electromagnetic interference before it reaches the wires. What does STP have that UTP doesn’t? Figure 7.4: UTP and STP cables UTP: Unshielded Twisted Pair STP: Shielded Twisted Pair 7.9
STP vs. UTP

STP : the metal braid or covering reduces interference , so it suits electrically noisy places such as factories. The price: it is more expensive and harder to handle , because it is thicker and heavier and the shield must be grounded properly. UTP : the cheapest cable and the easiest to install , which is why almost every office LAN uses it. The trade-off: it suffers from external electromagnetic interference (EMI) . So the choice depends on the environment: an ordinary office uses UTP, a site full of motors or heavy equipment uses STP (or fibre). UTP is not “worse” for every case: it is the default in LANs because it is cheap and easy. Compared with UTP, STP: A factory floor has heavy motors next to where the network cables will run. UTP or STP, and why? Why do most office LANs use UTP? Shielded Twisted Pair (STP) Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) ▪Metal braid or covering that ▪Cheapest type of cable reduces interference ▪Easiest type to be installed ▪More expensive ▪Suffers from external ▪Harder to handle (thick, Electromagnetic (EMI) heavy) interference
Categories of unshielded twisted-pair cables

The categories are standards for how good a twisted-pair cable is. A higher category supports a higher bandwidth (in MHz, how high a frequency it can carry) and so a higher data rate : CAT5e 100 MHz / 1 Gbps, CAT6 250 MHz / 1 Gbps, CAT6a 500 MHz / 10 Gbps , CAT7 600 MHz / 10 Gbps, CAT8 2000 MHz / 25 or 40 Gbps. CAT5e to CAT6a can be UTP or STP. From CAT7 upward the cable must be shielded . At such high frequencies, interference and crosstalk are too strong for unshielded pairs. Even then, the top speed only works over short runs: shielded CAT8 reaches 40 Gbps only up to about 24 m, which is why it is used inside data centres. Which is the first category in the table that is shielded only? CAT6a supports a maximum data rate of: A higher cable category supports a higher bandwidth and data rate. UTP connectors

RJ stands for Registered Jack . The RJ-45 is the 8-pin connector used on twisted-pair Ethernet cables. The female socket is in the NIC, switch or wall plate; the male plug is crimped onto the cable. (A phone cable uses the smaller RJ-11.) What does RJ stand for in RJ-45? Figure 7.5: UTP Connectors RJ=Registered Jack 7.12
The RJ-45 connector pinout

In 10 and 100 Mbps Ethernet, only four of the eight pins carry data. Pins 1 and 2 transmit: TD+ and TD- (Transmit Data positive and negative). Pins 3 and 6 receive: RD+ and RD- . Each signal uses a pair (+ and -) because the receiver reads the difference between the two wires, as in slide 8. Pins 4, 5, 7 and 8 are N/C , meaning No Connection or not connected: unused in 10/100 Ethernet. Gigabit Ethernet uses all eight pins, sending on all four pairs at once. In 10/100 Ethernet, which RJ-45 pins are used to transmit? Which pins receive data? What does N/C mean for pins 4, 5, 7 and 8? White/Orange White/Green Green 2 Orange Brown 3 TD+ : Transmit Data Positive value 1 TD- : Transmit Data Negative value RD+ : Receive Data Positive value 8 RD- : Receive Data Negative value The RJ-45 N/C: No Connection / Not Connected → unused pin Connector
Crossover cable

A crossover cable connects one end’s transmit pins (1, 2) to the other end’s receive pins (3, 6), and the other way round: 1 to 3, 2 to 6, 3 to 1, 6 to 2. That way, what one device sends lands on the other device’s receive pins. In a crossover cable, pin 1 at one end connects to which pin at the other end? Crossover Cable TD+ : Transmit Data Positive value TD- : Transmit Data Negative value RD+ : Receive White/Orange Data Positive value White/Green Orange Green Brown RD- : Receive Data Negative value
Ethernet cabling: straight-through vs. crossover

Straight-through cables wire each pin to the same pin at the other end (1 to 1, 2 to 2, 3 to 3, 6 to 6). They connect different kinds of device : a PC to a switch or hub , or a router to a switch or hub . This works because a switch already swaps transmit and receive internally, so the PC’s transmit pins meet the switch’s receive pins. Crossover cables connect the same kind of device : PC to PC , hub to hub , switch to switch , hub to switch . Two identical devices both transmit on pins 1 and 2, so a straight cable would connect transmit to transmit and nothing would be received; the crossover swaps the pairs. Memory rule: unlike devices use straight, like devices use cross. (Many modern ports detect and swap automatically, a feature called auto-MDIX, but exams expect the rule.) “Unlike → straight, like → cross.” (Router ↔ PC counts as “like”: both are end devices.) Which cable connects two PCs directly? Which cable connects a PC to a switch? Two switches are connected with a straight-through cable. A router connects to a switch. Which cable? Coaxial cable

Coaxial cable has a central copper wire (the inner conductor) inside a layer of insulation , surrounded by an outer conductor of copper mesh (braid or foil), and an outer plastic jacket . The outer conductor completes the circuit and shields the inner wire from interference, so coax carries higher frequencies than twisted pair. It is used for cable TV and was used in the old bus Ethernet (10Base5 thick coax and 10Base2 thin coax). Ch 4, slide 18 : Which media each Ethernet generation uses What is the outer copper mesh of a coaxial cable for? Coaxial cable is typically used for: Figure 7.7: Coaxial cable Copper wires (braid or foil) 7.16
Optical Fiber

An optical fibre has three layers from the inside out. The core is one or more very thin strands of glass or plastic, and it is what carries the light. Around the core is the cladding , glass or plastic with different optical properties from the core (a lower refractive index). That difference makes light that hits the boundary bounce back into the core instead of escaping. The outer jacket is plastic that protects the fibre from moisture, crushing and other damage. The layer of a fibre that keeps the light inside the core is the: Which part of a fibre actually carries the light? Optical Fiber consists of three concentric sections ◼ plastic glass or plastic jacket cover Fiber core and cladding ▪ Core: consists of one or more very thin strands or fibers made of glass or plastic ▪ Each fiber is surrounded by its own cladding, a glass or plastic coating that has optical properties different from the core ▪ Jacket: a plastic or other material acts as a layer to protect against moisture, crushing, and other environmental dangers.
Optical Fiber

The figure shows how light travels along a fibre: it reflects off the boundary between the core and the cladding again and again, zig-zagging down the core from the sender to the receiver. Because the light stays inside, very little signal is lost and nothing leaks out to be picked up by others. How does light travel along an optical fibre? Optical Fiber
Fiber Optics Properties

Fibre’s advantages: higher bandwidth (data rates of hundreds of Gbps); smaller size and lighter weight than copper; lower attenuation , so repeaters can be much farther apart, at least 50 km compared with about 100 m for UTP; no crosstalk , since no light leaks from one fibre to another; it is not affected by electromagnetic noise , because light isn’t disturbed by electrical fields; and it is highly secure , because no light leaks out for someone to tap. Its disadvantages: installing it needs special skills (fibres have to be cut, polished and joined precisely), and it is more expensive (the cable, connectors and equipment). A common exam trap lists “cheap” or “easy to install” as advantages of fibre; they are its disadvantages. Fiber is NOT cheaper or easier to install. Those are its two disadvantages. Which is a disadvantage of fibre-optic cable? Fibre-optic cable is not affected by electromagnetic noise. Give three advantages of fibre over copper. How far can fibre run without a repeater, according to the slide? Use the table as a decision tool: long distance, electrical noise or a high-voltage environment points to fibre; a short, ordinary office run points to UTP. Unguided media: wireless

The three unguided (wireless) media, from lowest to highest frequency : radio waves , microwaves , infrared . As the frequency goes up, signals become more directional and worse at going through walls. Order the unguided media from lowest to highest frequency. 7.2 Unguided Media: Wireless Radio Waves Microwaves Infrared
Wireless transmission waves (Figure 7.19)

With unguided media the signal travels through the air, so it is available to everyone who has a device that can receive it. That has two consequences: wireless is convenient (no cables, mobile devices), but anyone nearby can listen in, so security (encryption) matters much more than on a cable. Why does security matter more with unguided media? Figure 7.19 Wireless transmission waves Unguided media : signals are transmitted through air and are available to everyone who has a device that can receive them
Electromagnetic spectrum for wireless communication

The electromagnetic spectrum, frequency increasing from left to right : radio waves and microwaves from 3 kHz to 300 GHz (radio below 300 MHz, microwaves from 300 MHz to 300 GHz), then infrared from 300 GHz to 400 THz, then visible light from about 400 to 900 THz. A question that asks “which has the highest frequency?” among radio, microwave and infrared has infrared as the answer. Order by frequency: Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Light (“Really Many Infrared Lights”). Which has the highest frequency? Infrared’s frequency range is: Figure 2.25 Electromagnetic spectrum for wireless communication As we move from left to right, the frequency increases. Frequency tells us how many waves pass a point each second. 23
Radio waves

Radio waves are below 300 MHz . They are omnidirectional : the antenna sends the signal out in all directions , so the sending and receiving antennas don’t need to be lined up. They can travel long distances and pass through walls. That makes them suited to broadcasting : AM and FM radio and television, where one transmitter reaches everyone in the area. The downside is that anyone can receive them and nearby transmitters on the same frequency interfere. Radio waves are described as omnidirectional. This means: Which frequency range belongs to radio waves on the slide? Radio waves ▪ Less than 300 MHz ▪ Omnidirectional (signal propagates in all directions) ▪ Can Travel long distances ▪ Broadcast radio (AM,FM) ,TV
Note: radio waves

Radio waves are used for multicast communication: one sender, many receivers , as in radio and television broadcasting. Contrast this with microwaves (unicast) on slide 27. If a question describes one transmitter reaching many listeners, the answer is radio waves. Radio waves are used for which type of communication? Note Radio waves are used for multicast communications, such as radio and television
Microwaves

Microwaves run from 300 MHz to 300 GHz , the upper part of the radio range. Microwaves are unidirectional : they travel in a straight line, so the antennas must see each other , which is called line-of-sight propagation. That makes them good for point-to-point links, for example between two buildings to connect their LANs, with a dish on each roof pointing at the other. Because they are high frequency, they have a short wavelength and have trouble passing through walls : higher frequency means shorter wavelength, which means more difficulty getting through obstacles. Radio is OMNIdirectional; microwave is UNIdirectional (line of sight). Microwaves propagate: Higher frequencies pass through walls more easily. Two buildings want to connect their LANs wirelessly with dishes on their roofs pointing at each other. Which medium? Microwaves ▪ 300MHz to 300GHz (sub range from the Radio waves) ▪ Travel in one direction (Unidirectional = line-of-sight propagation = straight lines) ▪ Can be used for point to point for example between buildings to connect their LANs ▪ high frequency microwaves, difficult to pass walls (if receivers inside buildings) ▪ Higher frequency → shorter wavelength → more difficulty passing through obstacles such as walls. ▪ Used in Wireless networks, satellite, cellular phones. ▪ microwaves carry information through the air.
Note: microwaves

Microwaves are used for unicast communication: one sender to one specific receiver, as in cellular telephones , satellite networks and wireless LANs . The directional beam is what makes one-to-one links practical. Remember the pair: radio = multicast, microwave = unicast. Cellular telephones and satellite networks mainly use: Microwaves are used for which type of communication? Note Microwaves are used for unicast communication such as cellular telephones, satellite networks, and wireless LANs.
Infrared (IR Wireless)

Infrared runs from 300 GHz to 400 THz , just below visible light. It has a very large bandwidth , but it cannot penetrate walls , so it only works for short-distance, local communication, within one room. It also needs line of sight (directional): the remote has to point at the TV. It is used for local point-to-point links: remote controls , some wireless headphones and some wireless computer peripherals. Devices use the IrDA (Infrared Data Association) protocol. It cannot be used under the sun , because sunlight contains a lot of infrared that interferes with the signal. For most device-to-device links it has been replaced by Bluetooth , which uses radio and doesn’t need line of sight. Why can’t infrared be used outdoors in the sun? Which wireless medium cannot penetrate walls and is used in TV remote controls? Infrared links have mostly been replaced by: Which protocol do infrared devices use? Infrared (IR Wireless) ▪ 300GHz to 400THz ▪ Have a very large bandwidth ▪ Local- short distance communication because they cannot penetrate walls ▪ Line-of-sight propagation (directional) ▪ Used in local point-to-point Transmission ▪ Applications: remote controls, some wireless headphones, and some wireless computer peripherals. ▪ Use Infrared Data Association (IrDA) protocol ▪ Cannot be used under the sun because of the interference with the sun infrared rays ▪ Replaced by Bluetooth Technology
Note: infrared

Infrared’s one-line summary: short-range communication in a closed area , using line-of-sight propagation. The fact that it can’t leave the room is also an advantage: an infrared signal in one room doesn’t interfere with one in the next room, and it can’t be overheard from outside. Compare radio waves, microwaves and infrared by direction and typical use. An infrared signal in one room will not interfere with an infrared signal in the next room. Note Infrared signals can be used for short- range communication in a closed area using line-of-sight propagation.
