One section, 4.1 Ethernet . (On the course Slides page this deck is listed as Data Link Layer Part 3, because Ethernet is a data link layer protocol: it continues Chapter 3.) Chapter 4: Outline 4.1ETHERNET ◼ McGraw-Hill 2
IEEE standards

Ethernet is a LAN protocol at the data link layer , used in bus and star topologies. Classic Ethernet uses CSMA/CD as its medium access method: listen before sending, keep listening while sending, and stop and back off on a collision (Chapter 3 Part 2). Its history in two steps. The original Ethernet was developed in 1980 by three companies, Digital, Intel and Xerox , so it is called DIX Ethernet. In 1985 the IEEE Computer Society started Project 802 to write standards so that equipment from different manufacturers could work together; the current version is called IEEE Ethernet (802.3). Ch 3 Part 2, slide 17 : How CSMA/CD works Ch 1 Part 1, slide 32 : IEEE as a standards body Which access method does classic Ethernet use? DIX Ethernet was developed by: Why did IEEE start Project 802 in 1985? IEEE STANDARDS Ethernet: It is a LAN Data link layer protocol that is used in Bus and Star topologies and implements CSMA/CD as the medium access method ▪Original (traditional) Ethernet developed in 1980 by three companies: Digital, Intel, Xerox (DIX). ▪In 1985, the Computer Society of the IEEE started a project, called Project 802, to set standards to enable intercommunication among equipment from a variety of manufacturers. ▪ Current version is called IEEE Ethernet McGraw-Hill
Ethernet

The two frame formats are almost identical: preamble, destination address (6 bytes), source address (6), a 2-byte field, data (with padding) and the FCS (4). The one real difference is that 2-byte field: DIX uses it as a Type field (which network-layer protocol is inside), and IEEE 802.3 uses it as a Length field (how many bytes of data). Also, in 802.3 the eighth preamble byte is called the SFD (start frame delimiter). DIX → Type. 802.3 → Length. Same 2-byte position. The 2-byte field after the source address in an IEEE 802.3 frame is: What is the main difference between DIX and IEEE 802.3 frames? Ethernet ▪ Ethernet Frame format FCS FCS Frame formats. (a) DIX Ethernet , (b) IEEE 802.3. McGraw-Hill
802.3 MAC frame

The 802.3 frame field by field: preamble 7 bytes , SFD 1 byte , destination address 6 , source address 6 , length or type 2 , data and padding 46 to 1500 , CRC 4 . The preamble and SFD are added by the physical layer to wake up and synchronise the receiver, so they are not counted in the frame length: the frame officially runs from the destination address to the CRC. Frame fields and sizes: preamble 7 + SFD 1 (physical-layer header) · destination 6 · source 6 · type/length 2 · data 46–1500 · CRC 4. How long is the CRC field of an Ethernet frame? How long is each Ethernet address field? Figure 802.3 MAC frame McGraw-Hill
IEEE Ethernet

The MAC sublayer is specific to each LAN technology : for Ethernet it defines CSMA/CD ; for Token Ring it defines token passing . That is why there are different MAC standards for different LANs. The top sublayer, LLC (Logical Link Control), is IEEE 802.2 . It handles another part of framing and provides error and flow control if needed. It is the same for every LAN and makes the MAC sublayer transparent to the network layer: the layer above sees one LLC whether the LAN underneath is Ethernet or Token Ring, which lets different LANs interconnect. 802.3 = MAC for Ethernet. 802.2 = LLC on top, the same for every LAN. Ch 3 Part 2, slide 5 : The two data link sublayers Which IEEE standard is the LLC sublayer? Which sublayer is specific to each LAN technology? What does it mean that LLC makes the MAC sublayer transparent? IEEE Ethernet In IEEE 802.3 Ethernet Data link layer is split into two sublayers: ◼ Bottom part: MAC ◼ The subframe is called IEEE 802.3 ◼ Handles part of framing, MAC addressing, Medium Access control ◼ Specific implementation for each LAN protocol ◼ Defines CSMA/CD as the access method for Ethernet LANs and Token passing ◼ method for Token Ring. Top part: LLC (Logical Link Control) ◼ The subframe is called IEEE 802.2 ◼ Handles another part of Framing ◼ Provides error and flow control if needed ◼ It makes the MAC sublayer transparent ◼ Allows interconnectivity between different LANs data link layers ◼ McGraw-Hill
IEEE standard for LANs

The IEEE picture: one LLC (802.2) on top, shared by all LANs; below it several MACs (Ethernet, Token Ring, Token Bus), each with its own physical layers (different cables and speeds). Swapping the LAN technology only changes the MAC and physical parts. In the IEEE LAN standard figure, how many LLCs sit above the different MACs? Figure IEEE standard for LANs McGraw-Hill
Ethernet Frame

Preamble : 8 bytes of the pattern 10101010 . The alternating 1s and 0s let the receiver synchronise its clock with the sender’s before the real data starts. In IEEE 802.3 the eighth byte is the SFD , 10101011 : the final 11 says “the frame starts now”. Type (DIX): says which network-layer protocol is inside the data field, mostly IP, so the receiver knows which protocol to hand the data to: 0800 = IP, 0806 = ARP, 8137 = Novell IPX, 809B = AppleTalk. This lets one machine run several network-layer protocols at once (multiplexing). Type values start at 0x0600 = 1536 . Length (IEEE 802.3): the number of bytes in the data field, at most 1500 = 0x05DC . Because lengths stop at 1500 and types start at 1536, a receiver can tell which one it is: a value of 1500 or less is a length; 1536 or more is a type. CRC : a CRC-32 calculated over the frame. The receiver recomputes it; if it doesn’t match, the frame is discarded (Ethernet detects errors but doesn’t correct them; a higher layer can resend). Data : the packet from the upper layer. Pad : if the data is shorter than 46 bytes , zeros are added to reach 46. Example: 20 bytes of data needs 46 - 20 = 26 pad bytes. The two-byte field: ≤ 1500 → length (802.3); ≥ 1536 → type (DIX). The type value 0x0800 in an Ethernet frame means the payload is: If the data is only 20 bytes, how many pad bytes are added? An Ethernet receiver corrects a frame whose CRC check fails. The two-byte field in a received frame contains 1200 (decimal). It is: What is the preamble for? Ethernet Frame Preamble: ◼ 8 bytes with pattern 10101010 used to synchronize receiver, sender clock rates. ◼ In IEEE 802.3, eighth byte is start of frame (10101011) ◼ Addresses: 6 bytes (explained latter) ◼ Type (DIX) ◼ Indicates the type of the Network layer protocol being carried in the payload ◼ (data) field, mostly IP but others may be supported such as IP (0800), Novell IPX (8137) and AppleTalk (809B), ARP (0806) ) Allow multiple network layer protocols to be supported on a single machine ◼ (multiplexing) Its value starts at 0600h (=1536 in decimal) ◼ Length (IEEE 802.3): number of bytes in the data field. ◼ Maximum 1500 bytes (= 05DCh) ◼ CRC: checked at receiver, if error is detected, the frame is discarded ◼ CRC-32 ◼ Data: carries data encapsulated from the upper-layer protocols ◼ Pad: Zeros are added to the data field to make the minimum data length = 46 bytes ◼ McGraw-Hill
Ethernet address

An Ethernet (MAC) address is 6 bytes = 48 bits , written in hex like 06-01-02-01-2C-4B. It is flat , not hierarchical: unlike an IP address, no part of it says which network the device is on. It is burned into the NIC’s ROM at the factory. The first three bytes identify the vendor (for example Cisco 00-00-0C, Juniper 00-05-85); the last 24 bits are assigned uniquely by that company, so no two NICs in the world should share an address. A destination address can be unicast (one recipient), multicast (a group of stations, for example a conferencing application) or broadcast (all ones, every station). To tell unicast from multicast, look at the second hex digit from the left : even means unicast , odd means multicast . The source address is always unicast , because a frame always comes from exactly one device. Ch 1 Part 2, slide 28 : MAC = physical = NIC address An Ethernet MAC address is: A source MAC address can be a multicast address. What do the first three bytes of a MAC address identify? Ethernet address ▪ Six bytes = 48 bits ▪ Flat address not hierarchical ▪ Burned into the NIC ROM ▪ First three bytes from left specify the vendor. Cisco 00-00-0C, Juniper 00-05-85 and the last 24 bit should be created uniquely by the company ▪ Destination Address can be: ▪ Unicast: second digit from left is even (one recipient) ▪ Multicast: Second digit from left is odd (group of stations to receive the frame – conferencing applications) ▪ Broadcast (ALL ones) (all stations receive the frame) ▪ Source address is always Unicast McGraw-Hill
Ethernet address of a desktop PC Ethernet card

The address on this card is 00-60-97-98-1E-6B : it is printed on a sticker and stored in the card’s ROM. 00-60-97 is the vendor part; 98-1E-6B is the card’s own serial part. The second hex digit is 0, which is even, so it is a unicast address, as every NIC’s own address must be. The card’s address is 00-60-97-98-1E-6B. Which part identifies the vendor? McGraw-Hill
Note: unicast or multicast?

The precise rule: the least significant bit of the first byte decides the type: 0 = unicast , 1 = multicast . That bit is the last bit of the second hex digit (each hex digit is 4 bits, so the first byte is the first two digits). An even hex digit ends in binary 0 and an odd one ends in 1, which is why the even/odd shortcut works. Careful: it is the second hex digit , not the second byte. “Second digit” means the second HEX digit (part of byte 1), not the second byte. Which bit decides whether a MAC address is unicast or multicast? Note The least significant bit of the first byte defines the type of address. If the bit is 0, the address is unicast; otherwise, it is multicast. McGraw-Hill
Note: broadcast

The broadcast address, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF , has all 48 bits set to 1 . Since its multicast bit is also 1, broadcast is a special case of multicast : the group is “everyone”. Every station on the LAN accepts a broadcast frame (ARP requests use it). The broadcast address is a special case of a multicast address. The Ethernet broadcast address is: Note The broadcast destination address is a special case of the multicast address in which all bits are 1s. McGraw-Hill
Unicast and multicast addresses

The figure marks the deciding bit: the last bit of byte 1 (the first byte sent). Byte 1 is shown with that bit as 0 for a unicast address and 1 for a multicast address. The other 47 bits don’t affect the type. In the figure, the deciding bit for unicast or multicast is: Figure Unicast and multicast addresses McGraw-Hill
Example

Worked example, looking only at the second hex digit. (a) 4A :30:10:21:10:1A: A = 1010, even, so unicast . (b) 47 :20:1B:2E:08:EE: 7 = 0111, odd, so multicast . (c) FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF: all F, so broadcast . A quick list: even digits are 0 2 4 6 8 A C E; odd digits are 1 3 5 7 9 B D F. The destination address 01:00:5E:00:00:01 is: The destination address 3C:52:82:11:AA:07 is: The destination address 4B:12:00:9A:10:F0 is: Example Define the type of the following destination addresses: a. 4A:30:10:21:10:1A b. 47:20:1B:2E:08:EE c. FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF Solution To find the type of the address, we need to look at the second hexadecimal digit from the left. If it is even, the address is unicast. If it is odd, the address is multicast. If all digits are F’s, the address is broadcast. Therefore, we have the following: a. This is a unicast address because A in binary is 1010. b. This is a multicast address because 7 in binary is 0111. c. This is a broadcast address because all digits are F’s. McGraw-Hill
Ethernet frame

The figure shows the size limits. The payload (data) is at least 46 and at most 1500 bytes. The frame is therefore at least 64 bytes (512 bits) and at most 1518 bytes (12,144 bits) . Frame length counts destination (6) + source (6) + type/length (2) + data + CRC (4), but not the preamble and SFD. The Ethernet payload must be between: Figure : Ethernet frame 13.15
Note: frame length

Where 64 and 1518 come from: the header and trailer add 18 bytes (6 + 6 + 2 + 4). With the minimum data, 18 + 46 = 64 bytes (× 8 = 512 bits); with the maximum, 18 + 1500 = 1518 bytes (× 8 = 12,144 bits). The minimum exists for CSMA/CD: a frame must be long enough that the sender is still transmitting when news of a collision gets back to it, otherwise it couldn’t detect the collision. 18 bytes of overhead: 6 + 6 + 2 + 4. Add 46 → 64. Add 1500 → 1518. The minimum Ethernet frame length is: The maximum Ethernet frame length (without preamble) is: The minimum frame of 64 bytes is how many bits? Note Frame length: Minimum: 64 bytes (512 bits) Maximum: 1518 bytes (12,144 bits) McGraw-Hill
Ethernet evolution through four generations

Ethernet has gone through four generations, each 10 times faster than the last: Standard Ethernet 10 Mbps , Fast Ethernet 100 Mbps , Gigabit Ethernet 1 Gbps , 10 Gigabit Ethernet 10 Gbps . The frame format stayed the same throughout, which is why old and new equipment can work together. Fast Ethernet runs at: By how much does each Ethernet generation increase the speed? Figure Ethernet evolution through four generations McGraw-Hill
Ethernet Standards

Fast Ethernet (100Base-T, 100Base-F): star topology, 100 Mbps , over twisted pair or fibre . Gigabit Ethernet (1000Base-T, 1000Base-F): star, 1000 Mbps , twisted pair or fibre. 10 Gigabit Ethernet : star, 10,000 Mbps , and in these slides it uses fibre-optic cable only . All the newer generations use a star topology around a switch; the shared bus belongs to the original Standard Ethernet. In the slides, 10 Gigabit Ethernet uses only fibre-optic cable. Which topology do Fast, Gigabit and 10 Gigabit Ethernet use? Ethernet Standards Fast Ethernet (100 Base T, 100 Base F) ◼ Star topology ◼ 100 Mbps transmission rate ◼ media: twisted pair or fiber optic cable ◼ Gigabit Ethernet (1000 Base T, 1000 Base F) ◼ Star topology ◼ 1000 Mbps transmission rate ◼ media: twisted pair or fiber optic cable ◼ 10 Gigabit Ethernet (10gigabit F) ◼ Star topology ◼ 10000 Mbps transmission rate ◼ media: fiber optic cable only ◼ McGraw-Hill
10Base-T implementation

Read the name in three parts: 10 = 10 Mbps, Base = baseband (the cable carries one digital signal, not several modulated channels), T = twisted pair . 10Base-T connects each station to a hub or switch with two pairs of UTP: one pair to send and one to receive. Other letters: F = fibre, FX/SX/LX = kinds of fibre, CX = copper (shielded twisted pair). Name = speed + Base(band) + medium: T = twisted pair, F = fiber, X/LX/SX = fiber kinds, CX = copper. In “10Base-T”, the T stands for: What does “Base” mean in 10Base-T? Figure 10Base-T implementation switch 13.19
10Base-F implementation

10Base-F : 10 Mbps baseband over fibre-optic cable, with two fibres per station (one for each direction) running to the switch. Fibre lets the link be much longer and immune to electrical interference. 10Base-F uses which medium? Figure : 10Base-F implementation switch 13.20
Fast Ethernet implementations

Fast Ethernet has three main forms: 100Base-TX uses two pairs of Cat 5 UTP ; 100Base-FX uses two fibres ; 100Base-T4 uses four pairs of Cat 3 UTP (older, lower-quality cable, so it spreads the signal over more pairs). Which Fast Ethernet form uses four pairs of Cat 3 UTP? Figure Fast Ethernet implementations McGraw-Hill
Gigabit Ethernet implementations

Gigabit Ethernet: 1000Base-SX uses short-wave fibre (shorter distances), 1000Base-LX uses long-wave fibre (longer distances), 1000Base-CX uses copper (shielded twisted pair, very short runs), and 1000Base-T uses four pairs of UTP . Memory aid: S = short, L = long, C = copper, T = twisted pair. Which Gigabit Ethernet standard uses long-wave fibre? 1000Base-CX uses: Figure Gigabit Ethernet implementations McGraw-Hill
Full Duplex Operation

Traditional Ethernet is half duplex because of CSMA/CD: a station can either transmit or receive, but not both at the same time , since everyone shares one medium. In full duplex , a station can transmit and receive at the same time , so the throughput is doubled : 100 Mbps Ethernet becomes a theoretical 200 Mbps (100 each way), and 1 Gbps becomes 2 Gbps . Four changes are needed for full duplex: (1) full-duplex NICs in the stations; (2) two pairs of wire , one from host to switch and one from switch to host; (3) a switch , not a hub, as the central device (a hub repeats every signal to every port, so collisions are still possible); (4) each device connected point-to-point (a dedicated link) to the switch. Each station is then its own collision domain : nobody else shares its link, and sending and receiving use separate paths, so collisions can’t happen and CSMA/CD is no longer needed . A hub can’t do full duplex: it repeats to everyone, so collisions are still possible. 100 Mbps Ethernet in full-duplex mode has a theoretical rate of: Full-duplex Ethernet can use a hub as the central device. 6-1 CONNECTING DEVICES

Hosts and networks rarely work alone. Connecting devices link hosts together into a network, or link networks together into an internet. Because they work at different layers of the model, they differ in what they can read (bits, MAC addresses or IP addresses) and so in how cleverly they forward traffic. The three covered here are hubs , link-layer switches and routers . Which three connecting devices does the chapter discuss? 6-1 CONNECTING DEVICES Hosts and networks do not normally operate in isolation. We use ■ connecting devices to connect hosts together to make a network or to connect networks together to make an internet. Connecting devices can operate in different layers of the Internet model. We discuss three kinds of connecting devices: hubs, link-layer switches, and routers. McGraw-Hill 2
Three categories of connecting devices (Figure 6.1)

Each device covers the layers up to the one it works at. A hub works only at the physical layer. A link-layer switch works at the physical and data link layers. A router works up to the network layer. The higher a device goes, the more of each unit of data it understands, and the smarter its forwarding decisions. Ch 1 Part 2, slide 5 : Devices that don’t use all layers A link-layer switch operates in which layers? Which device works at the network layer? Figure 6.1 Three categories of connecting devices McGraw-Hill 3
Hubs

A hub is a physical-layer device : it works on bits , not frames, and doesn’t understand addresses at all. Stations plug into it in a physical star , but because it copies every signal to everyone, it behaves logically like a bus : one shared medium. When a bit arrives on one port, the hub sends it out of all the other ports , without any access method of its own and without filtering . Filtering would mean reading the frame’s destination MAC address and choosing the right port; a hub can’t do that. So every station receives every frame, and if two send at once their signals collide. Hubs can be chained to extend a network. In a star, the cable from a host’s NIC to the hub can be at most 100 m , so two hosts on the same hub can be at most 200 m apart, which is the maximum network length. A hub does not read MAC addresses at all; it only repeats bits. Each NIC checks the destination MAC address in the frame: B sees its own address and keeps the frame; C and D see someone else’s address and discard it. The filtering happens in the NICs, not in the hub, and the frame still used up everyone’s link. A sends a frame to B through a hub. Who discards the frame? A collision domain is the part of the network (the set of devices) in which, if two or more nodes transmit at the same time, their frames collide . On a hub, any two stations can collide, so the whole hub is one collision domain. A broadcast domain is the part of the network in which every device receives the other devices’ broadcast messages. A hub repeats broadcasts to everyone, so the whole hub is one broadcast domain too. Simple way to tell them apart: collision = who can crash into each other when sending ; broadcast = who hears each other’s broadcasts. Collision = who can crash into each other. Broadcast = who can hear each other’s shouting. Five PCs are connected to one hub. How many collision domains? Define collision domain and broadcast domain. Interconnecting with hubs

Joining LAN segments with hubs has one advantage : it extends the maximum distance between nodes, since each hub adds another 100 m of reach. The disadvantage : the separate segments’ collision domains merge into one large collision domain . Now a station in one department can collide with a station in another, and every station shares the same bandwidth, so performance drops as the network grows. Link-Layer Switches

A link-layer switch is a data link layer device. It also does physical-layer work: it regenerates the signal it receives, like a hub. The difference from a hub is that, as a data link device, the switch can read the MAC addresses (source and destination) in each frame, and use them to decide where the frame should go. What can a switch do that a hub can’t? Link-Layer Switches A link-layer switch (or switch) is a data link layer device. The switch physical-layer, regenerates the signal it receives. As a Data link layer device, the link-layer switch can check the MAC addresses (source and destination) contained in the frame. Multilayer Switch McGraw-Hill
Switches

Where a medium is still shared (a bus or a hub on one of its ports), the switch runs CSMA/CD before sending, so each switch port is a separate collision domain : a collision on one port doesn’t affect any other. And it filters : instead of copying a frame to every port, it forwards it only out of the port that leads to the destination MAC address . To know which port leads where, the switch keeps a forwarding table (switch table, MAC table). The table starts empty and fills automatically by learning from the frames passing through: nobody configures it. Each entry holds a host’s MAC address , the switch interface it is connected to, and the time the entry was created (old entries expire so the table stays current when hosts move). Switch learning process

Learning uses the source address. When a frame arrives, the switch looks up the frame’s source MAC in the table. If it isn’t there, the switch adds it with the interface the frame came in on : now it knows where that host is. If the source MAC is already there, the switch updates the interface if it has changed (the host moved to another port) and refreshes the record time. Forwarding uses the destination address. If the destination MAC is in the table, the switch compares its stored interface with the one the frame arrived on: if they are different , it forwards the frame out of the stored interface only; if they are the same , the destination is on the segment the frame came from, so the switch drops it (it has already arrived). If the destination is not in the table, the switch floods the frame out of every interface except the one it came in on , so it reaches the destination wherever it is. Broadcast and multicast frames are always sent out of all ports. Memory aid: the source teaches, the destination decides. Source teaches, destination decides. Loop problem in a learning switch

In a switched network , several switches connect the different parts of a LAN. For reliability , designers add redundant switches and links, so that if one link fails, another path still connects the hosts. The side effect: two hosts are now connected by more than one path , which forms a loop . Switches, unlike routers, have no way to notice that a frame has already been around the loop, so loops cause serious trouble (next slide). Why do switched networks have redundant links? When does the loop problem occur? Loop problem in a learning switch Switched network is a network where multiple swathes are used ■ to connect different LAN parts. In order to have reliable network, multiple switches and links are ■ used to connect different LAN parts (redundancy to increase reliability). This means that two host can be connected by multiple path. ■ Loop problem happens when there is more than one paths ■ between any two hosts, in a switched network. McGraw-Hill 14
Loop problem in a learning switch

With a loop, each switch that receives the flooded frame floods it again, so copies travel around the loop forever and multiply at every switch. There is nothing like a time-to-live in an Ethernet frame to stop them. Within seconds the copies use up all the bandwidth and the switches’ processing, and the network stops . That is a broadcast storm. The fix is the spanning tree protocol (STP), which removes the loops logically while keeping the redundant links available as backups. Loops in a switched network cause: Which protocol removes loops from a switched network? Which frames get flooded and can circulate in a loop? Also will do the same if the source MAC address is unicast but ■ is not stored in the forwarding table (Unknown Unicast). If the network has loops, then each switch once receives ■ broadcast, multicast, or unknown unicast will flood the frame through all other ports. This will replicate the same frame in the network continuously. ■ This is called broadcast storm and it will consume all the ■ network resources and then stops the network. Spanning tree protocol is used to eliminate the loops ■ McGraw-Hill 15

Spanning tree: blocking ports

The idea comes from graph theory: for any connected graph there is a spanning tree , a subset of the links that still connects every node but has no closed loops . STP finds such a tree for the switches. STP removes the loops logically , not physically: no cable is unplugged. It does this by blocking certain ports. A blocked port doesn’t forward ordinary data frames, but it still passes the spanning tree protocol’s own frames , so the switches keep monitoring the network. If something changes (a link fails), STP runs again and a blocked port can become a forwarding port , so the redundant link takes over as a backup. STP doesn’t remove cables; it logically blocks ports. Ports blocked by spanning tree forward no frames at all. A blocked port can become a forwarding port again if the network changes. How does spanning tree remove loops? Blocking Port ▪ For any connected graph there is a spanning tree that maintains connectivity but contains no closed loops ▪ Loops are logically disabled by the spanning tree algorithm ▪Some ports will be blocked by spanning tree to eliminate loops ▪Blocked ports do not forward data frames but forward special frames belong to spanning tree algorithm ▪Blocked ports will become forwarding port if any change happen in the network that cause spanning tree protocol to run again. McGraw-Hill

How the spanning tree is found: first one switch is chosen as the root (here S1). Then, for every other switch, STP keeps only the shortest path to the root (costs of 1 from a switch to a LAN and 0 from a LAN to a switch). The links that are on some shortest path are kept; the rest are blocked. What is the first step in finding the spanning tree? Figure 6.7 Finding the shortest path and the spanning tree for a switch. Data frames never leave through a blocked port. After the spanning tree algorithm, which ports are blocked in the example? Some switch features

Where the medium is shared, a switch implements CSMA/CD. It isolates collision domains : each segment (port) is its own collision domain, so there are fewer collisions and a higher total throughput , because several pairs of hosts can communicate at the same time. However, a switch still forwards a broadcast frame to every device on the whole switched network: a switched network without VLANs is a single broadcast domain . Only routers (or VLANs) split broadcast domains. More advantages: better performance and security , because a frame only goes out of the port leading to its destination; wider coverage , with no limit on the size of LANs joined by switches; and it is transparent and plug-and-play : installing or removing a switch, or moving a host, doesn’t require reconfiguring anything. A network of switches with no VLANs forms how many broadcast domains? A switch isolates broadcast domains. What does it mean that a switch is transparent? Switch sends the ■ frame through the port to which the receiving device is connected. Increases geographical coverage ■ No limit on the size of the LANs connected through switches ■ Transparent: installing or removing a switch does not require the stations ■ networking software to be reconfigured. (“plug-and-play”): no configuration necessary at installation of switch or ■ when a host is removed from one of the LAN segments McGraw-Hill
Isolated collision domains

Every switch port is its own collision domain. The lower part of the figure adds full duplex: with separate transmit and receive paths on each link, there are no collisions at all , so CSMA/CD isn’t needed. The network built with hubs only (three hubs, four PCs) is one collision domain and one broadcast domain . If the bandwidth is 100 Mbps, the four hosts share it, so each gets an average maximum effective bandwidth of 100/4 = 25 Mbps . The same network built with switches : count the links between a switch port and another device. There are 6 (four PC links and two switch-to-switch links), so 6 collision domains . With no router, it is still 1 broadcast domain . Each host now has its own link, and in full duplex it can send and receive at once, so each gets up to 200 Mbps (100 each way) instead of 25 Mbps, and CSMA/CD isn’t needed. The same 4 hosts on full-duplex switches each get up to: Three switches and four PCs are joined by 6 links. No need for CSMA/CD McGraw-Hill
Some switch features – cont’d

They do MAC address recognition and frame forwarding in hardware (special chips), which is why they are fast. There are two types. Store-and-forward : the switch receives the whole frame , buffers it briefly, checks it for errors (the CRC), and only then sends it to the right output. That is reliable, but the buffering adds delay . Cut-through : since the destination address is at the start of the frame, the switch starts sending the frame to the output port as soon as it has read that address (if the output is free), without buffering the rest. That means no buffering delay, but no error checking : a corrupted frame is forwarded anyway. Memory aid: store-and-forward = safe but slow; cut-through = quick but careless. Store-and-forward = Safe but Slow. Cut-through = Quick but Careless. Which switching type checks the frame for errors before forwarding? Cut-through switching starts forwarding after reading the: What is the drawback of store-and-forward switching? Buffering will cause some delay. Cut-through: based on the fact that the destination address ■ appears at the beginning of the MAC frame, so once the address is recognized the frame is directly sent to the appropriate output line if the output buffer is empty (no need to buffer it). 🡺 no buffering delay 🡺 NO ERROR CHECKING McGraw-Hill
Routers

A router works at the network layer , so it deals with packets , not frames. It connects LANs and WANs, even ones using different protocols. Each router interface has both a physical (MAC) address and an IP address . Routers isolate both collision domains and broadcast domains : a router doesn’t forward broadcasts from one interface to another, so each router interface is a separate broadcast domain . A router behaves like a normal station on each network it joins, but it has more than one logical (IP) address, one per interface. It forwards packets based on the destination IP address , exchanges routing information with other routers, and uses a routing algorithm to find the best route . If it has no route to the destination, it discards the packet, unlike a switch, which floods frames it doesn’t know where to send. Ch 8, slide 3 : How routers build their tables Which device isolates both collision and broadcast domains? A router floods a packet whose destination is not in its routing table. Virtual LANs

The network here has 12 collision domains and 3 broadcast domains (three subnets, each on its own switch, joined by a router). Now suppose a new user belongs to subnet 1, but there is no space in subnet 1’s room, only in the room where subnet 3 is. The alternative is a VLAN (virtual, or logical, LAN): create the subnets, which are broadcast domains, in software instead of by physical wiring. The user plugs into the nearby switch, and the switch is told that this port belongs to subnet 1. Advantages Of VLAN

Three advantages. Lower cost and installation time : moving a station to another group is done in software instead of rewiring. More security : a group that needs high security can be put in its own VLAN, so no one outside can communicate with it directly, and its broadcast messages aren’t received by other VLANs. Virtual workgroups : stations in different physical places can be put in the same broadcast domain, for example people from different departments working on one project. Give three advantages of VLANs. People from three departments on different floors work on one project and need to share broadcasts. Which VLAN advantage is this? Advantages Of VLAN : Reduce cost and installation time ■ Instead of physically moving a station to another segment or another ■ switch, it can be moved by software. Increase security: ■ A group of users needing a high security can be put into a VLAN so ■ that NO users outside the VLAN can communicate with them. Stations belong to the same group can send broadcast messages that ■ will NOT be received by users in others VLAN groups Creating Virtual Workgroups ■ Stations located at physically different locations can be added easily to ■ the same broadcast domain so that they can send broadcast messages to one another. EXAMPLE: people from different departments working on the same ■ project McGraw-Hill

The deck covers the network layer’s job of moving packets: its duties; the two ways of switching packets ( virtual circuit and datagram ); IPv4 addresses (notation, classes, network/host/broadcast addresses); masks and subnetting ; how a host gets its settings ( DHCP ) and finds a neighbour’s MAC address ( ARP ); the IPv4 header and fragmentation ; and NAT . Subnetting is the biggest calculation topic in the course, and it only becomes fast with practice. The whole method fits in four steps, shown in the tip below: work out the block size from the mask, find the multiple of the block at or below the address (the network), the next multiple minus one (the broadcast), and everything in between (the usable hosts). Every subnetting slide below works through this with numbers. Subnet in four lines: block size = 256 - the interesting mask octet · network = the multiple of the block at or below the address · broadcast = next network - 1 · usable = network + 1 to broadcast - 1. A subnet mask’s interesting octet is 240. What is the block size in that octet? Chapter 7: Outline

Three sections: 7.1 services (the duties of the network layer), 7.2 packet switching (virtual circuit vs. datagram), and 7.4 Internet Protocol version 4 (addressing, subnetting, DHCP, ARP, the header, fragmentation, NAT). Section 7.4 is most of the deck and most of the exam weight. Chapter 7: Outline 7.1 Services ◼ 7.2 Packet Switching ◼ 7.4 Internet Protocol V4 ◼ McGraw-Hill 2
Network layer duties

The network layer has five duties. Internetworking : joining different networks into one internet. Addressing : giving every interface a unique, global logical address (the IP address). Routing : finding the best path through the networks. Packetizing : wrapping the transport layer’s data in a packet. Fragmenting : cutting a packet into smaller pieces when the next network can’t carry it whole. Framing is not on the list: it belongs to the data link layer. Ch 1 Part 2, slide 33 : Network layer overview Which is NOT a duty of the network layer in the slides? Network layer duties McGraw-Hill
Packetizing

Packetizing is the first duty: at the source, the network layer encapsulates the payload (a segment from the transport layer) in a packet; at the destination it decapsulates it and hands the payload up. Its promise is to carry the payload from source to destination without changing it or using it , exactly like a postal service delivering a parcel without opening it. What does packetizing promise about the payload? Packetizing The first duty of the network layer is definitely packetizing: encapsulating the payload in a network- layer packet at the source and decapsulating the payload from the network-layer packet at the destination. In other words, one duty of the network layer is to carry a payload from the source to the destination without changing it or using it. The network layer is doing the service of a carrier such as the postal office, which is responsible for delivery of packages from a sender to a receiver without changing or using the contents. McGraw-Hill
Routing and forwarding

Routing is the planning job: routers run routing protocols with each other to find the best paths, and store the results in a decision-making table called the routing table . It happens in the background, before and while packets flow. Forwarding is the action taken for each packet: when a packet arrives on one interface, the router looks up the destination in its table and decides which interface to send it out of . A comparison: routing is planning the trip on a map; forwarding is turning the right way at each junction. Routing is planning the trip; forwarding is turning at each junction. Ch 8, slide 3 : Routing protocols fill the table Deciding which output interface to send an arriving packet on is: Running protocols to find the best paths and fill the routing table is: Routing and Forwarding Routing: Finding the best path (route) by running routing protocols to fill a decision-making table (called routing table). Forwarding: The action applied by the router when it receives a packet at one of its interfaces. It will decide from which other interface the packet should be sent. McGraw-Hill
Packet switching

From routing and forwarding we can see that the network layer does a kind of switching . A router is, in fact, a switch : it connects one of its input ports to one (or more) of its output ports for each packet, just as an electrical switch connects an input to an output so current can flow. Why can a router be called a switch? PACKET SWITCHING From the discussion of routing and forwarding in the previous section, we infer that a kind of switching occurs at the network layer. A router, in fact, is a switch that creates a connection between an input port and an output port (or a set of output ports), just as an electrical switch connects the input to the output to let electricity flow. McGraw-Hill
Switching

There are two approaches to packet switching. The virtual-circuit approach is connection-oriented : a path is set up first, and all packets of a message follow it. The datagram approach is connectionless : every packet is handled on its own and may take its own path. The Internet uses the datagram approach. The two packet-switching approaches are: SWITCHING McGraw-Hill
Packet switching: virtual-circuit approach

In a connection-oriented service, the virtual-circuit approach , all packets of a message are related: they belong to one connection. Before any are sent, a virtual connection is set up that fixes the path. After setup, all packets follow the same path , so they arrive in order. Each packet carries the source and destination addresses and also a flow label , a virtual circuit identifier that tells each switch which virtual path the packet belongs to. In the virtual-circuit approach, what does each packet carry besides the addresses? In a virtual-circuit network, all packets of a message follow the same path. Packet switching – Virtual-Circuit Approach • In a connection-oriented service (also called virtual- circuit approach), there is a relationship between all packets belonging to a message. • Before all datagrams in a message can be sent, a virtual connection should be set up to define the path for the datagrams. • After connection setup, the datagrams can all follow the same path. • In this type of service, not only must the packet contain the source and destination addresses, it must also contain a flow label, a virtual circuit identifier that defines the virtual path the packet should follow. McGraw-Hill
Virtual-circuit setup

During setup, a connect request travels switch by switch (SW1, SW2 … SWn) to the destination, and each switch reserves what the connection needs: buffer space, bandwidth, delay limits . A connect confirm comes back, and data can flow. Why is it called virtual ? Because the switches, buffers and lines are shared by packets of many connections; nothing is physically dedicated to one connection, unlike a real telephone circuit. A virtual circuit is called virtual because resources are shared by packets of several connections. What is reserved in every switch during virtual-circuit setup? Virtual circuit Setup Parameters such as buffer, bandwidth, delay requirements were set in every switch along the path during setup Connect Connect Connect request request request SW SW … SW 1 2 n Connect Connect Connect confirm confirm confirm Question: why called virtual-circuit? Because resources, e.g., switches, buffers and lines, are shared by packets from multiple connections. McGraw-Hill
A virtual-circuit packet-switched network

All packets of the message follow the same virtual circuit, here through R1, R3 and R4, so they arrive in order (1, 2, 3, 4), and no router has to make a fresh routing decision for each one. In a virtual-circuit network, packets of a message arrive: Figure: A virtual-circuit packet-switched network McGraw-Hill
Flow of one packet in an established virtual circuit

How a packet follows its circuit: each switch keeps a table that maps (incoming port, incoming label) → (outgoing port, outgoing label) . The packet arrives with label 14; the switch looks it up, swaps the label to 66 and sends it out of the stored port; the next switch swaps 66 for 22, and so on. Labels only have meaning between two neighbouring switches, so they can be short. What does a switch do with the label of a packet in an established virtual circuit? Figure : Flow of one packet in an established virtual circuit McGraw-Hill
Delay in a circuit-switched network

Delay in a circuit-switched or virtual-circuit network has three phases: connect (setup, the request going out and the confirm coming back), data transfer , and disconnect (teardown). Setup and teardown add delay before the first bit of data moves, but after that each packet just follows the established path with no per-packet routing decisions. Which phases make up delay in a circuit-switched network? Figure: Delay in a circuit-switched network McGraw-Hill
Packet switching: datagram approach

When the Internet began, the network layer was designed, for simplicity, to give a connectionless service: each packet is handled independently , with no relationship to any other packet. The network layer is only responsible for delivering each packet from source to destination. Packets of the same message may or may not take the same path, and keeping them in order (if needed) is left to the transport layer. In the datagram approach, each packet is: Packet switching – Datagram Approach When the Internet started, to make it simple, the network layer was designed to provide a connectionless service in which the network-layer protocol treats each packet independently, with each packet having no relationship to any other packet. The idea was that the network layer is only responsible for delivery of packets from the source to the destination. In this approach, the packets in a message may or may not travel the same path to their destination. McGraw-Hill
Note: the Internet is connectionless

The one line to remember: communication at the network layer in the Internet is connectionless . IP is a datagram protocol: no setup, no reserved path, each packet routed on its own. Communication at the network layer in the Internet is: Note: Communication at the network layer in the Internet is connectionless. McGraw-Hill
A connectionless packet-switched network

A connectionless network has no handshaking (no setup phase). Each packet is sent and routed independently and may follow a different path, so each packet must carry the full source and destination addresses : there is no label linking it to a connection. Consequences: there is no setup delay ; packets are not guaranteed to arrive in the order sent (in the figure, packet 3 overtakes packet 2); and it is robust : if a router crashes, only the packets inside it are lost, and later packets simply take another path. This is what the Internet uses. Compare the virtual-circuit and datagram approaches. In a datagram network, packets are guaranteed to arrive in order. Why is a datagram network robust? Figure : A connectionless packet-switched network Connectionless service :No handshaking, each packet is sent and routed independently and can follow different paths to reach to the destination. The full address of the source and destination must be attached to each packet. ▪ No setup delay ▪ Packets are not guaranteed to arrive in the order they were sent ▪ Robust: If a router crashes only packets inside the router will be lost, other packets can follow other path ▪ Used in the Internet McGraw-Hill
Delay in a datagram network

Delay in a datagram network is the transmission time plus the waiting (queuing) time at each router , with no setup phase . But each router must look up the destination for every packet, and different packets may wait different amounts of time. Which delay does a datagram network NOT have? Figure: Delay in a datagram network McGraw-Hill
Forwarding in a connectionless router

A connectionless router’s forwarding table maps destination address → output interface . When a packet arrives, the router reads only its destination address , finds it in the table, and sends the packet out of the matching interface (here, interface 2). The source address plays no part in the decision. A connectionless router chooses the output interface using: Figure : Forwarding process in a router when used in a connectionless network SA DA Data SA DA Data McGraw-Hill
Addressing

The network-layer address in TCP/IP is the IP address . An IPv4 address is 32 bits , written as 4 octets (bytes). IP addresses are unique (each connection to the Internet has a different address) and universal (every host that wants to connect to the Internet must accept the same addressing system). To avoid conflicts they are managed by a non-profit organisation, ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers). ICANN assigns blocks to regional authorities , which assign them to ISPs , which assign them to customers. ICANN also manages DNS (domain names). An IPv4 address is: Which organisation manages IP addresses globally? Addressing The address in the network layer of the TCP/IP model is called Internet ◼ Address or IP address An IP address is a 32-bit address ◼ The IP addresses are unique (each connection has a different address) ◼ and universal (must be accepted by any host wants to connect to the internet). Consists of 4 octets (bytes) ◼ Network IP addresses are managed by a nonprofit organization called ◼ ICANN (International Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) to avoid conflicts. Assigns addresses to regional Authorities which assign numbers to ISPs ◼ Assigns and manages DNS (Domain Name System) ◼ McGraw-Hill
Note: the IPv4 address space

With 32 bits there are 2³² = 4,294,967,296 possible IPv4 addresses, about 4.3 billion. That sounds like a lot, but the world has far more devices than that, which is why classless addressing, private addresses with NAT, and IPv6 exist. How many addresses does the IPv4 address space contain? The address space of IPv4 is 232 or 4,294,967,296. McGraw-Hill
Different notations in IPv4 addressing

The same address can be written two ways. Binary : 10000000 00001011 00000011 00011111. Dotted decimal : each 8-bit group converted to decimal and separated by dots: 128.11.3.31. Dotted decimal is what people use; binary is what you need for masks and subnetting. 10000000 00001011 00000011 00011111 in dotted decimal is: Figure 7.4 different notations in IPv4 addressing McGraw-Hill 20
Example 1: binary to dotted-decimal

To convert binary to dotted decimal, convert each 8-bit group separately using the bit weights 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 and add the weights of the 1 bits. 10000001 = 128 + 1 = 129; 00001011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11; 11101111 = 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 239. So (a) is 129.11.11.239, and (b) is 249.155.251.15. 11000000 10101000 00000001 00001010 in dotted decimal is: 10101100 00010010 00000011 00010100 in dotted decimal is: Example 1 Change the following IP addresses from binary notation to dotted- decimal notation. a. 10000001 00001011 00001011 11101111 b. 11111001 10011011 11111011 00001111 Solution We replace each group of 8 bits with its equivalent decimal number (see Appendix B) and add dots for separation: a. 129.11.11.239 b. 249.155.251.15 McGraw-Hill
Example 2: dotted-decimal to binary

To convert decimal to binary, go through the weights 128, 64, 32 … 1: if the weight fits into what is left, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0. 111: 128 doesn’t fit (0); 64 fits (1, leaves 47); 32 fits (1, leaves 15); 16 doesn’t (0); 8 fits (1, leaves 7); 4 (1, leaves 3); 2 (1, leaves 1); 1 (1). So 111 = 01101111 . Always write 8 bits per octet, with leading zeros. 172.16.5.9 in binary is: Example 2 Change the following IP addresses from dotted- decimal notation to binary notation. a. 111.56.45.78 b. 75.45.34.78 Solution We replace each decimal number with its binary equivalent (see Appendix B): a. 01101111 00111000 00101101 01001110 b. 01001011 00101101 00100010 01001110 McGraw-Hill
Example: find the error

Each octet is 8 bits, so it must be between 0 and 255 . 75.45.301.14 is invalid because 301 > 255. Other errors to look for: more or fewer than four octets (1.2.3.4.5), a mix of binary and decimal, and leading zeros such as 045 (not allowed in dotted decimal). Which is a valid IPv4 address? Example Find the error, if any, in the following IP address: 75.45.301.14 Solution In dotted-decimal notation, each number is less than or equal to 255; 301 is outside this range. McGraw-Hill
Hierarchy in addressing

An IP address has two parts. The prefix (the first n bits) identifies the network the host is on; the suffix (the remaining 32 - n bits) identifies the connection of the host to that network. Setting the suffix to all 0s gives the network address (also called network or block ID). The suffix is the host ID , but strictly it identifies the host’s interface (its connection), not the machine itself. Setting the host part of an address to all 0s gives: The host ID identifies the host’s interface (its connection to the network), not the machine itself. Figure 7.5 Hierarchy in addressing Network + Host: Complete IP address Network Address: Host part set to 0 Network (block) ID: identifies the network to which the host is connected Host ID: identifies the interface of the network connection to the host not the host itself McGraw-Hill 24
IP address with a router

An IP address belongs to an interface , not to a machine. A router connected to three networks has three interfaces , and so three IP addresses , each one from the network that interface is on. A laptop with both Wi-Fi and Ethernet connected likewise has two IP addresses. A router connected to three networks has three IP addresses. McGraw-Hill
Note: five classes

In the original classful addressing, the address space was divided into five classes: A, B, C, D and E . The class decided how many bits were network and how many host, so it decided how big each network was. How many classes does classful addressing have? Note: In classful addressing, the address space is divided into five classes: A, B, C, D, and E. McGraw-Hill
Occupation of the address space in classful addressing

How the address space was shared out: class A took half of all addresses ( 50% ), class B a quarter ( 25% ), class C an eighth ( 12.5% ), and classes D and E 6.25% each. Class A had very few, huge blocks, which wasted many addresses: one of the reasons classful addressing was abandoned. What share of the IPv4 address space did class A occupy? Occupation of the address space in classful addressing McGraw-Hill 27
Finding the classes in binary and dotted-decimal notation

The class can be read from the first bits : A starts with 0 , B with 10 , C with 110 , D with 1110 , E with 1111 . Or from the first byte in decimal: A 0–127 , B 128–191 , C 192–223 , D 224–239 , E 240–255 . Remember the upper limits 127, 191, 223, 239, 255 and you can classify any address instantly. First-byte limits: 127 / 191 / 223 / 239 / 255. An address starting with 190 is class: An address whose first bits are 110 is class: Finding the classes in binary and dotted-decimal notation McGraw-Hill
Classful Addressing

Class A : first bit 0, first byte 0–127. 8 network bits and 24 host bits , so each block has 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 addresses, minus 2 usable (the all-0s host part is the network address x.0.0.0 and the all-1s host part is the broadcast address x.255.255.255), giving 16,777,214 hosts. The valid blocks are 1 to 126 (126 blocks): 0.x.x.x is reserved (0.0.0.0 means the default route, or a device that doesn’t know its own address yet), and 127.x.x.x is reserved for loopback (a host sending to itself, for testing, as in ping 127.0.0.1). All class A blocks are allocated (large networks). Class B : first bits 10, first byte 128–191. 2 fixed bits + 14 network bits give 2¹⁴ = 16,384 blocks ; 16 host bits give 2¹⁶ = 65,536 addresses per block, 65,534 usable. All allocated (medium networks). The 127.x.x.x block is reserved for: How many usable host addresses does one class B block have? How many class B blocks are there? Classful Addressing ▪ Class A ▪ Range in decimal 0 - 127 ▪ Start with binary 0 ▪ 8 bits reserved for network portion ▪ Number of bits for host : 32-8= 24 ▪ Number of complete IP addresses in each block is 224=16777216 – 2 (all zeros host - network address (x.0.0.0), and all ones – broadcast address (x.1.1.1) ▪ Valid Range 1.x.x.x to 126.x.x.x (126 valid blocks) ▪ Address 0.x.x.x is reserved (0.0.0.0 default route): a device does not yet know its own IP address ▪ (127) block reserved for loopback ▪ All allocated to organizations or other entities (large networks) ▪ Class B ▪ Start with binary 10 ▪ 214=16384 blocks (network addresses) ▪ Range 128.x.x.x to 191.x.x.x ▪ Number of addresses in each block is 216=65536 – 2 (all zeros host, and all ones) ▪ 2 fixed bits(10) + 14 network bits + 16 host bits = 32 bits ▪ All allocated to organizations or other entities (medium networks) McGraw-Hill
Classful Addressing

Class C : first bits 110, first byte 192–223. 3 fixed bits + 21 network bits give 2²¹ = 2,097,152 blocks ; 8 host bits give 256 addresses per block, 254 usable. Nearly all allocated (small networks). Class D is for multicast : one sender to a specific group of receivers. Its first four bits are 1110, and it has no network/host split : the whole address names a group. Private IP addresses are used inside local networks and are not routable on the public Internet: 10.0.0.0–10.255.255.255 , 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0–192.168.255.255 . Anyone may use them internally; to reach the Internet, they are translated by NAT (slide 82 onward). Watch the 172 range: 172.16 to 172.31 only, so 172.32.x.x is public. This deck, slide 84 : Private addresses and NAT Which address is private? Class D addresses are used for: How many usable hosts are in one class C block? Classful Addressing Class C ◼ Start with binary 110 ◼ Range 192.x.x.x to 223.x.x.x ◼ ▪ 221=2097152 blocks (network addresses) ▪ 3 fixed bits(110) + 21 network bits + 8 host bits = 32 bits Number of addresses in each block is 2^8=256 – 2(all zeros host, and all ◼ ones) class Nearly all allocated (Small networks) ◼ Class D ◼ ▪ Multicast addresses: (one sender sends data to a specific group of receivers) ▪ First four bits: 1110 ▪ No network/host hierarchy Range Total Private IP addresses are used inside local networks 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 224 and are not directly 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 220 routable on the public Internet. 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 216 McGraw-Hill
Sample internet

The figure shows a sample internet mixing networks of different classes (A, B and C), joined by routers and WAN links. Each network has its own network address, and each router interface takes an address from the network it is on. In the sample internet, what does each router interface get? Figure : Sample internet Class B Class C Class A McGraw-Hill
Summary of IPv4 address classes
Class E (first bits 1111) is used for: Classful Addressing McGraw-Hill
Find the class of each address:

Classifying in binary: (a) 00000001 … starts with 0 , so class A . (b) 11110011 … starts with 1111 , so class E . Read only as many leading bits as you need: stop at the first 0. An address in binary starts 11110011… Its class is: Example 3 Find the class of each address: a. 00000001 00001011 00001011 11101111 b. 11110011 10011011 11111011 00001111 Solution See the procedure in Figure 19.11. a. The first bit is 0; this is a class A address. b. The first 4 bits are 1s; this is a class E address. McGraw-Hill
Find the class of each address:

The address 227.12.14.87 is class: The address 245.10.1.1 is class: Example 4 Find the class of each address: a. 227.12.14.87 b. 252.5.15.111 c. 134.11.78.56 Solution a. The first byte is 227 (between 224 and 239); the class is D. b. The first byte is 252 (between 240 and 255); the class is E. c. The first byte is 134 (between 128 and 191); the class is B. McGraw-Hill
Example: network address (class A)

Finding the classful network address: work out the class, keep the network bytes and set the host bytes to 0. 23.56.7.91 is class A (first byte 23), so only the first byte is network: the network address is 23.0.0.0 . The classful network address of 23.56.7.91 is: Example 5 Given the address 23.56.7.91, find the network address. Solution The class is A. Only the first byte defines the netid. We can find the network address by replacing the hostid bytes (56.7.91) with 0s. Therefore, the network address is 23.0.0.0. McGraw-Hill
Example: network address (class B)

132.6.17.85 is class B (first byte 132), so the first two bytes are network: the network address is 132.6.0.0 . For class C, keep three bytes: 201.14.78.65 → 201.14.78.0. The network address of 201.14.78.65 (classful) is: Example 6 Given the address 132.6.17.85, find the network address. Solution The class is B. The first 2 bytes defines the netid. We can find the network address by replacing the hostid bytes (17.85) with 0s. Therefore, the network address is 132.6.0.0. McGraw-Hill
Example: class from a network address

Going the other way: given the network address 17.0.0.0, the netid is only one byte , so it is class A (which also matches 17 being in 0–127). A network address 17.0.0.0 belongs to class: Example 7 Given the network address 17.0.0.0, find the class. Solution The class is A because the netid is only 1 byte. McGraw-Hill
Network, Host, and Broadcast Addresses

Every network has three kinds of address. The network address : host part all 0s, for example 192.168.10.0; it names the network and can’t be given to a host. Host addresses are everything between: here 192.168.10.1 (the first usable) to 192.168.10.254 (the last usable). The directed broadcast address has the host part all 1s, 192.168.10.255; a packet sent to it reaches every host on that network. In 192.168.10.0/24, which is NOT a usable host address? Network, Host, and Broadcast Addresses • Within each network there are three types of IP addresses: Network address 1. Host addresses 2. Directed Broadcast address 3. Host Network Portion Portion Network address 192 168 10 0 192.168.10.0 11000000 10101000 00001010 00000000 First address 192 168 10 1 192.168.10.1 11000000 10101000 00001010 00000001    Last address 192 168 10 254 192.168.10.254 11000000 10101000 00001010 11111110 Direct Broadcast address 192 168 10 255 Directed 192.168.10.255 11000000 10101000 00001010 11111111 Broadcast McGraw-Hill
Broadcast in IPv4

A directed broadcast address is used to send a message to all nodes of a specific network , usually a network different from the sender’s. It is the network ID with all 1s in the host part (192.168.10.255 for 192.168.10.0/24). Routers forward it towards that network. Because attackers have used it to flood networks (denial-of-service attacks), it is usually blocked. A directed broadcast address has: Routers forward packets sent to a directed broadcast address. Broadcast in IPv4 Directed Broadcast address ◼ Broadcast address for a message that is directed to ALL nodes in a ◼ specific network different from the source device network It has the net id and all ones in binary in the host portion ◼ Net ID All ones in binary Will be forwarded by routers ◼ It is usually blocked as it can be used for denial of service attacks ◼ McGraw-Hill
Broadcast in IPv4

A limited broadcast address is for a message to all nodes on the sender’s own network . It is 255.255.255.255 , and routers never forward it , because routers separate broadcast domains. DHCP uses it, for example, when a new host doesn’t yet know its own network. The trap: the directed broadcast (192.168.10.255) can cross routers; the limited broadcast (255.255.255.255) cannot. Directed broadcast (e.g. 192.168.10.255) CAN cross routers; limited broadcast 255.255.255.255 cannot. Which broadcast address is never forwarded by routers? The directed broadcast address of 192.168.10.0/24 is: Broadcast in IPv4 Limited Broadcast Address ◼ Broadcast address for a message to be received by all nodes within the same network as the ◼ source device Routers do not forward a message that has limited broadcast address as destination ◼ address (Routers isolate broadcast domains) 255.255.255.255 Routers stop Limited broadcast address McGraw-Hill
Note: the network address is assigned

In classful addressing, what an organisation is given is a network address , which stands for the whole block: for example 132.6.0.0 gives it every address from 132.6.0.0 to 132.6.255.255. In classful addressing, what is an organisation given? Note: In classful addressing, the network address is the one that is assigned to the organization. McGraw-Hill
Subnet Mask

Questions the slide answers. Why a mask? To calculate the network (subnet) address of any IP address: the mask marks which bits are network. Default mask vs. subnet mask : the default (class) mask belongs to classful addressing, where the class decides the network size. A subnet mask belongs to classless addressing, where the mask decides it. Valid lengths : a subnet mask must be longer than the default mask of the address’s class (it borrows host bits), and no longer than /30 (a /31 or /32 would leave no usable hosts, since 2 addresses are always lost to network and broadcast). How to use it : do a bitwise AND of the address and the mask. Shortcut, octet by octet: where the mask is 255 , copy the address octet; where it is 0 , write 0; for the one octet in between, convert both to binary, AND them, and convert back. Mask octets to know by heart: 128 · 192 · 224 · 240 · 248 · 252 · 254 · 255. What is the longest valid subnet mask according to the slide? Using the shortcut, what do you write where the mask octet is 255? In classless addressing, the mask (not the class) defines the network address. Why network address is needed? Case 1: A device is sending a packet

Case 1, a host sending. The network layer needs the destination’s network address to decide: is the destination on the same network as me, or another one? It ANDs the destination address with its own mask and compares the result with its own network address. If it is the same network , the packet is handed to the data link layer to deliver directly to the destination (using the destination’s MAC). If it is another network , the data link layer is asked to send the frame to a router , the default gateway (the router interface on the sender’s own network), which will forward it. Example: 192.168.10.10/24 sending to 192.168.20.5: 192.168.10.0 ≠ 192.168.20.0, so it goes to the gateway. Host 192.168.10.10/24 sends to 192.168.20.5. What does its network layer do? Host 192.168.10.10/24 sends to 192.168.10.77. Where does the frame go? Why network address is needed? Case 1: A device is sending a packet Default Gateway • For a sending device, network layer needs the network address for the destination to check if the destination is connected to the same network as the sender or to another network. • If the destination is connected to the same network, then network layer will give the data link layer the packet to deliver it. • If the destination is NOT connected to the same network, then network layer will ask data link layer to send it to a Router to be delivered (The default Gateway). Subnetwork benefits

The benefits of subnetting: less overall traffic (each subnet is its own broadcast domain, so broadcasts stay local); smaller networks are easier to manage and troubleshoot; more control over the address space ; and more security , since traffic between subnets passes through a router where it can be filtered. The steps, with the example 192.168.1.0/24 into 5 subnets. (1) 5 - 1 = 4. (2) 4 in binary is 100. (3) That is 3 bits . (4) Add them to the default mask: /24 + 3 = /27 = 255.255.255.224. (5–6) The weight is the value of the last 1 bit of the mask in its octet: 224 = 11100000, the last 1 is worth 32 (also 256 - 224). (7–10) The first subnet is the original address, 192.168.1.0/27; keep adding 32: .32, .64, .96, .128, .160, .192, .224, and stop before passing 255. That gives 8 subnets of 32 addresses each. Write the weight 2 of the first non-zero bit in the subnet mask starting from the rightmost octet 2. The first subnet is the original network address with the subnet mask 3. The next subnet is the original network address after adding the weight, obtained in (2), to the value of the first non-zero octet in original network address from the right 4. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)

DHCP is an application-layer protocol (it runs over UDP) that gives a host, including a diskless computer, its IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server automatically. It is an application protocol even though the settings it hands out belong to the network layer, which is a common trap. The DHCP server keeps two databases . The static database maps MAC addresses to permanent IP addresses (used for diskless workstations and servers that must always have the same address). The dynamic database is a pool of unused addresses handed out temporarily. When a host asks, the server checks the static database first. If the host’s MAC isn’t there, it takes a free address from the dynamic pool and gives it as a temporary address with a lease : the address is the host’s only for a set period of time , so unused addresses aren’t wasted. When the lease expires, the host must return the address or renew the lease. DHCP lives in the application layer even though it configures network-layer settings. DHCP is a protocol of which layer? A DHCP lease means the address is given for a limited period. Which DHCP database does the server check first? IPv4 datagram fields

The header is at least 20 bytes (without options) and at most 60. The total length field covers header + data, up to 65,535 bytes. Identification , flags and fragment offset are used for fragmentation and reassembly . A packet can be fragmented at any node between the source and the destination, but reassembly happens only at the destination , because fragments may take different routes and only the destination is sure to receive them all. Time to live (TTL) stops lost packets from circling between routers forever (in a routing loop). The source sets it to a starting value (depending on its operating system); each router subtracts 1 and checks it, and if it reaches 0 the packet is dropped . The protocol field holds a code saying what is carried in the data (TCP, UDP, a routing protocol), so the destination knows whom to hand it to. The header checksum checks for errors in the header only , not the data (the transport layer checks the data). It is recomputed at every router , because the header changes on each hop: at least the TTL is decremented. The IPv4 checksum does not cover the data. What happens when a router decrements TTL to 0? The protocol field says which upper protocol the payload belongs to. The source writes the code and the destination uses it to deliver the data to the right protocol. The IPv4 protocol value for UDP is: Figure 7.14 The value of the protocol field ▪ Protocol field determines to which of the Transport layer and Network layer protocols) the data in the network packet should be delivered to. ▪ Each protocol is given a value as shown below in the table. ▪ The source will insert the corresponding value in the protocol field ▪ The destination network layer will use the value to deliver the data to the right protocol McGraw-Hill 74
Fragmentation

A datagram crosses many different networks. At each router it is taken out of the incoming frame (decapsulated), processed, and put into a new frame for the next network (encapsulated). The format and size of that frame depend on the next network: a router joining a LAN to a WAN receives LAN frames and sends WAN frames. If the next network’s frames are smaller than the datagram, the datagram has to be cut up. Why might a router have to fragment a datagram? Fragmentation A datagram can travel through different networks. Each ◼ router decapsulates the IP datagram from the frame it receives, processes it, and then encapsulates it in another frame. The format and size of the received frame depend on the protocol used by the physical network through which the frame has just traveled. The format and size of the sent frame depend on the protocol used by the physical network through which the frame is going to travel. For example, if a router connects a LAN to a WAN, it receives a frame in the LAN format and sends a frame in the WAN format. McGraw-Hill 75
MTUs for some networks

Each network has its own MTU (maximum transfer unit, the largest payload its frame can carry): Hyperchannel 65,535; Token Ring 17,914 (16 Mbps) and 4,464 (4 Mbps); FDDI 4,352; Ethernet 1,500 ; X.25 576; PPP 296. Ethernet’s MTU of 1500 bytes is the same number as Ethernet’s maximum data field from Chapter 4. The MTU of Ethernet is: MTUs for some networks McGraw-Hill
Maximum Transfer Unit

Every link-layer protocol has its own frame format, and one of its properties is the MTU : the maximum size of data that can be put in one frame. So the network-layer packet must be no larger than the MTU of the network it is about to cross. If it is larger, it must be fragmented into pieces that fit. MTU is: Maximum Transfer Unit Each link-layer protocol has its own frame format. ◼ One of the features of each format is the maximum ◼ transfer size (MTU) which puts a limit on the maximum data size that can be encapsulated in a frame The network layer packet size must be less than the ◼ maximum size McGraw-Hill 77
Fragmentation

The same point from the router’s side: each router re-encapsulates the datagram in the frame type of the next network. If the next network’s MTU is smaller than the datagram, the router fragments it before sending. A router connects a LAN to a WAN. What frame format does it send on the WAN side? Fragmentation A datagram can travel through different networks. Each router decapsulates the IP datagram from the frame it receives, processes it, and then encapsulates it in another frame. The format and size of the sent frame depend on the protocol used by the physical network through which the frame is going to travel. For example, if a router connects a LAN to a WAN, it receives a frame in the LAN format and sends a frame in the WAN format. McGraw-Hill
Fragmentation and Reassembly

Fragmentation can take place at the sender and at any router . Reassembly takes place only at the final receiver . A fragment can even be fragmented again by a later router with a smaller MTU; each fragment travels as an independent datagram with its own header. Where can fragmentation happen? Fragmentation and Reassembly ▪ Fragmentation takes place at the sender and routers ▪ Reassembly takes place at the receiver ONLY. Fragment Reassemble at source at destination Source Router Destination Fragment IP at router IP Network Network McGraw-Hill
Flags used in fragmentation

The flags field has three bits: reserved, D (do not fragment) and M (more fragments). M = 1 means this is not the last fragment; M = 0 means it is the last one (or the packet was never fragmented). D = 1 means the packet must not be fragmented : if such a packet reaches a router whose next link has a smaller MTU, the router drops it (and reports an error with ICMP). A fragment with M = 0 is: A router fragments a packet even if D = 1 when it is bigger than the MTU. Flags used in fragmentation M=1 means the packet is not the last fragment M=0 means the packet is the last fragment D=1 means Do not fragment the packet If the packet arrives to a router with Do not fragment flag equals ‘1’ and the router has to forward the packet but its size is larger than the link MTU, the router will drop the packet McGraw-Hill
Example of checksum calculation

The header checksum is the same one’s-complement checksum as in Chapter 3, calculated over the header only : the header is split into 16-bit words, they are added with wrap-around, and the sum is complemented (giving CBB0 in the example). If a router finds an error, it drops the packet. It is recomputed at every router , because fields such as the TTL change at every hop. Ch 3 Part 1, slide 42 : The Internet checksum What does the IPv4 header checksum cover? Network Address Translation (NAT)

NAT (Network Address Translation) maps between private (local) and public (global) IP addresses. It lets a whole site use private addresses internally and only a few public addresses (at least one) to communicate with the rest of the world. NAT maps between: Network Address Translation (NAT) NAT: is A technology that can provide the mapping ◼ between the private (local) and Public (global) IP addresses NAT: The technology allows a site to use a set of private ◼ addresses for internal communication and a set of global (Public) Internet addresses (at least one) for communication with the rest of the world. McGraw-Hill
Network Address Translation (NAT)

Why NAT is needed: business customers and many home users stay connected all the time , so each needs an address all the time, and an ISP doesn’t have enough addresses for all its customers (a class B block supports only 65,536). The solution is a NAT-enabled router between the site and the ISP: everyone inside uses private addresses, and the router translates them to its own public address on the way out. Why do ISPs need NAT for always-connected customers? Network Address Translation (NAT) How To save IP addresses; ◼ For business customers and many home users (ADSL), they want to ◼ stay connected continuously ➔ each user must have its own IP address ➔ total number of IP number an ISP can provide will not be enough to cover all customers (for example, class B block can support 65536 only) Solution is using NAT enabled router ◼ NAT: is A technology that can provide the mapping ◼ between the private (local) and Public (global) IP addresses NAT: The technology allows a site to use a set of private ◼ (local) addresses for internal communication and a set of global (Public) Internet addresses (at least one) for communication with the rest of the world. McGraw-Hill
Private addresses and the NAT router

The private ranges again: 10.0.0.0/8 , 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 , 192.168.0.0/16 . Inside the site in the figure, hosts use private addresses 172.18.3.1 to 172.18.3.20 . The NAT router’s outside interface has the one public address given by the ISP, 200.24.5.8 . To the Internet, the whole site looks like that one address. In the NAT figure, what address does the outside world see for the whole site?
