Address translation

How the translation works. For an outgoing packet, the NAT router replaces the source address: private 172.18.3.1 becomes public 200.24.5.8 . For an incoming reply, it replaces the destination address: 200.24.5.8 becomes 172.18.3.1 again. Out → change the source; in → change the destination. For an outgoing packet, a NAT router changes the: For an incoming reply, a NAT router changes the: Figure : Address translation Web Server 25.8.2.10 McGraw-Hill
Translation table

How does the router know which inside host a reply is for? When the outgoing packet passes, it records an entry in a translation table (private address 172.18.3.1 ↔ destination 25.8.2.10). When a reply comes from 25.8.2.10, the router finds the entry and changes the destination back to 172.18.3.1. How does the NAT router know which inside host a reply belongs to? Figure : Translation Destination McGraw-Hill
Network Address Translation (NAT)

In practice: the company connects to its ISP through a NAT-enabled router that has the one unique public address. The router keeps a translation table (up to 65,536 entries), and each row has four fields : private source address , source port number , destination address , and a NAT port number that must be unique. The port numbers are what let many inside hosts share one public address: each connection gets its own NAT port, so replies can be told apart. Every machine inside has a unique private address , usually from 10.x.y.z. In the basic version shown, NAT won’t let more than one inside host contact the same destination at the same time, since the replies couldn’t be told apart. Which is NOT a field in a NAT translation table row? Network Address Translation (NAT) How does it work? ◼ A company is connected to the ISP through a router with NAT software ◼ (router is called NAT enabled router). The router has a unique IP address given to the company by the ISP NAT router maintains a translation table that has 65536 entries. Each ◼ row has four fields: Private source address, source port number, destination address, NAT port number (should be unique) Every machine within a company has a unique IP address selected from ◼ the set of private addresses usually (10.x.y.z) If a computer inside the company want to connect to a computer outside ◼ the network, such as a Web server, the NAT router receives the packet from the computer NAT will NOT allow more than one host to contact same destination ◼ McGraw-Hill
Advantages of using NAT

Advantages of NAT: saves IP addresses (one public address for all the site’s devices, so no need for a range from the ISP); internal addresses can be changed without telling the outside world ; the site can change ISP without renumbering its devices; and it acts like a firewall : an outside computer can’t start a connection to an inside one, because there is no table entry until the inside computer makes contact (and Internet routers won’t forward packets addressed to private IPs). You can browse and download, but nobody outside can open a connection to a port on your machine. Give three advantages of NAT. Why does NAT act like a firewall? Advantages of using NAT No need to be allocated range of global addresses from ISP: just one ◼ global IP address is used for all devices ➔ save IP address can change addresses of devices in local network without notifying ◼ outside world can change ISP without changing addresses of devices in local network ◼ Can be used as firewall. A computer on an external network cannot ◼ connect to your computer unless your computer has initiated the contact. You can browse the Internet and connect to a site, and even download a file; but somebody else cannot use your IP address to . (** Internet routers do connect to a port on your computer not recognize and forward packets with private destination IP addresses) McGraw-Hill

Chapter 8: Outline

Two sections: 8.1 introduction (the general idea, graphs, static vs. dynamic routing, routing tables and forwarding) and 8.2 routing algorithms (distance vector, link state, and autonomous systems). Which section covers distance vector and link state? Chapter 8: Outline 8.1 Introduction ■ 8.2 Routing Algorithms ■ 2
Routing (IP routing)

A routing protocol is software in the network layer that implements a routing algorithm. It has two jobs. Routing : filling and updating the routing tables by finding the best (shortest) path from each source to each destination. Forwarding : deciding which output interface each incoming packet goes out of, by looking up the routing table. Routing builds the table; forwarding uses it. Ch 7, slide 5 : Routing vs. forwarding Filling and updating routing tables by finding best paths is called: Which statement about a routing protocol is correct? Routing (IP routing) Routing Protocol: determines the best path (route) that the ■ packets should follow to arrive to the desired destination Routing Protocols: A software in the network layer that ■ implements routing algorithms and responsible for: Filling and updating routing tables (by finding the ■ shortest paths (best path) from each source to each destination) This part is called Routing Deciding which output interface an incoming packet ■ should be transmitted on (by referring to the routing table). This part is called Forwarding
8-1 INTRODUCTION

The Internet has a huge number of routers and hosts, far too many for every router to know a path to every network by one single algorithm. So unicast routing is done hierarchically : in several steps, with different algorithms at different levels (inside each autonomous system, and between autonomous systems; see slide 34). Why is Internet routing hierarchical? 8-1 INTRODUCTION Unicast routing in the Internet, with a large number of ■ routers and a huge number of hosts, can be done only by using hierarchical routing: routing in several steps using different routing algorithms. 4
8.1.1 General Idea

In unicast routing a packet moves hop by hop from source to destination, each router using its forwarding table. The source host doesn’t need a forwarding table: it just sends any packet for another network to its default router . The destination host doesn’t need one either: it receives the packet from its own default router. So only the routers that join the networks together need real forwarding tables. Why doesn’t a source host need a full forwarding table? 8.1.1 General Idea In unicast routing, a packet is routed, hop by hop, from its ■ source to its destination by the help of forwarding tables. The source host needs no forwarding table because it ■ delivers its packet to the default router in its local network. The destination host needs no forwarding table either ■ because it receives the packet from its default router in its local network. This means that only the routers that glue together the ■ networks in the internet need forwarding tables. 5
An Internet as a Graph

To find the best route, an internet is modelled as a graph : a set of nodes connected by edges . Each router is a node, and each network between two routers is an edge. Each edge also has a cost , so it is a weighted graph . Finding the best route then becomes a standard graph problem: finding the least-cost path. In the graph model of an internet, routers are: Why is an internet modelled as a weighted graph? An Internet as a Graph To find the best route, an internet can be modeled as a ■ graph. A graph in computer science is a set of nodes and edges ■ (lines) that connect the nodes. To model an internet as a graph, we can think of each ■ router as a node and each network between a pair of routers as an edge. An internet is, in fact, modeled as a weighted graph, in ■ which each edge is associated with a cost. 6
An internet and its graphical representation (Figure 8.1)

The figure turns a real internet (routers and LANs) into a weighted graph with nodes A to G and a cost on each edge. The same graph is used in all the distance vector and link state examples later, so it is worth getting familiar with it. In the A–G graph, what does a number on an edge represent? Figure 8.1 An internet and its graphical representation 7
Graph representation of a network

The cost comes from a metric , which can be: the number of hops (routers or networks crossed), geographic distance, link delay, capacity (speed), reliability, or a combination. Different routing protocols use different metrics (RIP counts hops; OSPF usually uses bandwidth). A good path is the one with the minimum total cost from source to destination: the sum of the costs of all its links. A path with more hops can still be the best if its links are cheaper. Which is NOT listed as a possible link cost metric? A good path is the one with: Graph representation of a network Graph nodes are routers Cost ■ Edge Graph edges are physical links (network) ■ Each link has a value which represents the ■ “cost” of sending a packet across the link The cost is assigned based on a metric ■ ▪ Cost metric can be: ▪ Number of networks (hops or routers) ▪ Geographic distance ▪ Link delay ▪ Capacity (speed) Node ▪ Reliability ▪ Combination of the above How to select a “good” path??? ■ Good path is the one with minimum cost = ■ Total cost from src to dest
Routing Algorithms Classifications

Static routing: routes change slowly over time. Shortest paths are computed offline by a special computer running the routing algorithm, and the results are entered manually by the administrator into the routing tables. It can’t update automatically if the network changes or a link fails; someone has to edit the tables. It suits small networks. Dynamic (adaptive) routing: each router learns the state of the network by communicating with its neighbours (the routers directly connected to it), and fills its own routing table from what it learns. It adapts automatically to changes and failures, at the cost of more complexity in the router (more processing, memory and protocol traffic). Static routes do NOT update automatically after a failure. Static routing updates automatically when a link fails. Compare static and dynamic routing. What is the cost of dynamic routing? Routing Algorithms Classifications Static ■ Routes change slowly over time ■ Shortest paths are precomputed offline by a special computer ■ running the routing algorithm Resulted information is entered manually by the administrator into ■ the routing tables Can not update automatically if there is a change in the network or ■ failure Used in small networks ■ Dynamic (adaptive) ■ Each router or host learns the state of the network by ■ communicating with its neighbours (routers that are directly connected to each other). Based on the collected information, each node (router) can fill its ■ routing table More complexity is added to the router ■
Routing algorithm: dynamic route operation

In dynamic routing, the routing protocols on neighbouring routers maintain and exchange routing information: each router sends updates to its neighbours, and each uses the updates it receives to keep its own routing table current. In dynamic routing, what do neighbouring routers exchange?
How to reduce number of entries in the routing table?

Three ways to control what goes into the routing table. Network-specific routing lists a destination network (one row covers every host on it). Host-specific routing lists a single destination host (used when one host needs a special path). Default routing provides one row that covers every destination not listed . Network-specific and default routes keep the table short. Which method keeps one row for every destination not listed? How to reduce number of entries in the routing table? Network-Specific routing (Destination Network IP Address is listed in ■ the table) Host Specific Routing ( Destination Host IP Address is listed in the ■ table) Default Routing ■
Host-specific versus network-specific method

With host-specific routing, router S’s table needs a row for every host on network N2 (A, B, C, D, each via R1). With network-specific routing, one row for N2 via R1 covers all of them, so the table is much smaller. Host-specific rows are only worth having for special cases, such as testing or security. Listing one entry for a whole destination network instead of each host is: Host-specific versus network-specific method Destination Next Hop N1 Directly Connected A R1 B R1 C R1 Destination Next Hop D R1 N1 Directly Connected N2 R1 IP addresses S Network Address N1 Network Address N2
Default Route

The default route is used when the destination’s network isn’t found in the routing table. It is written 0.0.0.0/0 : a mask of /0 matches every address, so this row covers “any other destination”. In the example, router S sends traffic for N1 directly, traffic for N2 to R1, and everything else (the rest of the Internet) to R2 . The default route is written as: In router S’s table, where does a packet for an unlisted network go? Forwarding of IP packets

Forwarding means placing a packet on its route to its destination. This section adds the role of IP addresses: the router uses the destination address and the masks in its table to pick the next hop. Forwarding means: We discussed the concept of forwarding at the network layer earlier in this chapter. In this section, we extend the concept to include the role of IP addresses in forwarding. As we discussed before, forwarding means to place the packet in its route to its destination.
Destination Address Forwarding

Destination-address forwarding , the traditional approach used today: when a host has a packet to send, or a router receives one to pass on, it looks up the destination address in its forwarding table to find the next hop (and the interface to reach it). In destination-address forwarding, the router looks up: Destination Address Forwarding We first discuss forwarding based on the destination address. This is a traditional approach, which is prevalent today. In this case, forwarding requires a host or a router to have a forwarding table. When a host has a packet to send or when a router has received a packet to be forwarded, it looks at this table to find the next hop to deliver the packet to.
Classful addressing routing table

How a router uses a table with masks: for each row, it applies the row’s mask to the destination address (AND) and compares the result with the row’s destination. If it matches, it forwards the packet to that row’s next hop through its interface. If no specific row matches, it uses the default row. If there is no default either, it sends a “host unreachable” error back to the sender (with ICMP). In this table, the /32 row is a host-specific route (all 32 bits must match one address) and the /0 row is the default . What happens if no row matches and there is no default route? A /32 row in a routing table is a: Classful addressing routing table 0.0.0.0 ▪ When a packet arrives: ▪ Apply all the available masks to the IP destination address ▪ If a match is found in the destination address column, the packet has to be forwarded to the next hop IP address through the corresponding interface ▪ If no match is found, send the packet through the default interface ▪ Otherwise, a message “host unreachable error” is . sent back to the sender
Example

Destination 193.14.5.22 : apply each mask in turn. With /24, 193.14.5.22 AND 255.255.255.0 = 193.14.5.0 , which matches the 193.14.5.0/24 row, so the packet goes out through interface m2 . This is a network-specific match. Using the table, a packet for 14.5.6.7 leaves through: Example 0.0.0.0 Using the table above, the router receives a packet for destination 193.14.5.22. For each row, the mask is applied to the destination address until a match with the next-hop address is found. In this example, the router sends the packet through interface m2 (network specific).
Example

Destination 200.34.12.34 : applying each row’s mask gives no match with any listed destination, so the router uses the default row and sends the packet out through m0 . A packet for 200.34.12.34 matches none of the rows. It leaves through: Example 0.0.0.0 Using the table above, the router receives a packet for destination 200.34.12.34. For each row, the mask is applied to the destination address, but no match is found. In this example, the router sends the packet through the default interface m0.
Example

Destination 192.16.7.1 : it matches the /32 row exactly (every bit equal), so the packet goes out through m0 . This is a host-specific match: the route applies to that one host only. A packet for 192.16.7.1 leaves through m0 because: Example 0.0.0.0 Using the table above, the router receives a packet for destination 192.16.7.1. For each row, the mask is applied to the destination address until a match with the destination address is found. In this example, the router sends the packet through interface m0 (host specific).
Example: router R1’s networks

Router R1 has four interfaces, each attached to a network: m0 to 180.70.65.128/25 , m1 to 201.4.16.0/22 , m2 to 180.70.65.192/26 , m3 to 201.4.22.0/24 . The rest of the Internet is reached through another router, 180.70.65.200 , on m2’s network. How does R1 reach the rest of the Internet? Forwarding table for router R1

R1’s forwarding table. The rows are sorted from the longest mask to the shortest : /26, /25, /24, /22, with the default 0.0.0.0/0 last. A “–” in the next-hop column means the network is directly connected (deliver straight to the destination host). The router tries the rows in order and uses the first match , which is always the longest matching prefix : the most specific route wins, and the default is only used when nothing else matches. Longest prefix first, default last. Why are R1’s rows sorted from the longest mask to the shortest? (2) Apply /25: 130 AND 128 = 128, giving 180.70.65.128 , which matches the /25 row, so the packet goes out through m0 (directly connected, so straight to the host). The same method with 201.4.22.35: /26, /25 fail; /24 gives 201.4.22.0, a match, so m3. The result is 180.70.65.128, which does not match the corresponding network address. 2. The second mask (/25) is applied to the destination address. Destination 25.8.2.10 . Apply /26 → 25.8.2.0 (no match); /25 → 25.8.2.0 (no); /24 → 25.8.2.0 (no); /22 → 25.8.0.0 (no). R1 receives a packet for 25.8.2.10. Walk through the forwarding steps. Show the forwarding process if a packet arrives at R1 with the destination address 25.8.2.10. Solution The router performs the following steps: 1.The first mask (/26) is applied to the destination address. The result is 25.8.2.0, which does not match the corresponding network address. 2. The second mask (/25) is applied to the destination address. The result is 25.8.2.0, which does not match the corresponding network address. 3. The second mask (/24) is applied to the destination address. The result is 25.8.2.0, which does not match the corresponding network address. 4. The second mask (/22) is applied to the destination address. The result is 25.8.0.0, which does not match the corresponding network address. In this example, the router sends the packet to the default route. The next-hop address will be 180.70.65.200 through interface m2.
Shortest Path Routing

Shortest-path routing algorithms find the path between two nodes with the least cost : the path whose link costs add up to the smallest total among all possible paths. There are two main families: distance vector , based on the Bellman-Ford algorithm, and link state , based on Dijkstra’s algorithm. Link-state routing uses which algorithm? Distance-vector routing is based on: Shortest Path Routing ▪ Algorithms used to determine the shortest path between two nodes according to some cost condition. ▪ The shortest path is the path with the least cost (the sum of the cost of the links on the path is minimum over all possible paths between the source and destination) ▪ Two main algorithms to find the shortest path between any two nodes ▪ Distance Vector (Bellman-Ford Algorithm ) ▪ Link State – (Dijkstra’s Algorithm)
Distance Vector (DV) Routing

In distance vector (DV) routing, each router keeps a distance vector table : its current distance to every possible destination in the domain, measured by the chosen metric (often hops, or bandwidth, or delay). It sends this whole vector to its neighbours (directly connected routers) periodically , or when something changes. A router recalculates its vector when it receives a neighbour’s vector with different information than before, or when it notices that a link to a neighbour has gone down or up (a topology change). The new distances come from the neighbours’ vectors, choosing the cheapest option for each destination, and the routing table follows directly from the vector. Examples of distance vector protocols: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) and EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol). Memory aid: DV = tell your neighbours about the whole world ; LS = tell the whole world about your neighbours . DV = “tell your NEIGHBOURS about the WHOLE world”. LS = “tell the WHOLE world about your NEIGHBOURS”. Which is a distance-vector protocol? In distance vector routing, a router sends its vector to: When does a DV router recalculate its vector? Distance Vector (DV) Routing ▪ Basic idea: each network node maintains a Distance Vector (DV) table containing the distances from itself to ALL possible destination nodes in the domain. ▪ Distances are based on a chosen metric (Metric: usually number of hops, bandwidth, delay) ▪ Router transmits its distance vector table to each of its neighbors (directly connected to it) periodically or when there is a change. ▪ A router recalculates its distance vector when: It receives a distance vector table from a neighbor containing different ▪ information than before. ▪ It discovers that a link to a neighbor has gone down or up (i.e., a topology changes). ▪ Distances to all destinations are computed using information from thereceived neighbors’ distance vectors. ▪ The DV calculation is based on minimizing the cost to each destination. From its DV, a router can directly derive its routing table. ■ ▪ Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) and Routing Information Protocol (RIP) are examples of distance vector protocols
The first-round distance vectors

Round 1 : each node knows only the cost to its directly connected neighbours ; every other destination is ∞ (unreachable, as far as it knows yet). The vectors then improve round by round as neighbours exchange them. In the first round of DV, what does each node know? Link State Routing

It puts these costs into a packet, the link-state packet (LSP) , and sends it by flooding to all the other routers in the routing area, not just its neighbours. Congestion Control

Congestion happens when the load on the network (the number of segments sent into it) is greater than its capacity (the number it can handle). Routers’ queues fill up, packets are delayed and then dropped. Congestion control is the set of techniques that keep the load below the capacity , for example by slowing down the senders when signs of congestion appear. Compare with flow control: flow control protects the receiver from a fast sender; congestion control protects the network . Flow control protects the RECEIVER; congestion control protects the NETWORK. TCP Sequence Number

When the connection is set up, each side announces its initial sequence number (ISN) , which is a random number (so old segments from a previous connection can’t be confused with new ones). The first segment’s sequence number is the ISN. Every later segment’s sequence number = the previous segment’s sequence number + the number of bytes the previous segment carried . Once the connection is established, both sides can send data to each other. Every segment must be acknowledged . Flow control in TCP uses windows , called sliding windows , to stop a receiver from being overwhelmed. User Datagram Protocol (UDP)

UDP is unreliable : it has no flow control and no error control , so a datagram can be lost, arrive out of order, be duplicated, or be corrupted . Its checksum covers the entire datagram but is optional . If the checksum shows an error, UDP doesn’t try to recover; it simply discards the datagram. The application takes full responsibility for dealing with errors. It does use port numbers to multiplex and demultiplex data to and from the application layer. Its advantages: it is simple , has minimum overhead (an 8-byte header), and has no connection delay (no handshake). Its services are just process-to-process delivery and (optional) error checking, which on error only discards the message. Domain Name System

DNS is the Internet’s directory service: a client-server application that maps host names (like www.psu.edu.sa) to their IP addresses . This mapping is called name resolution (also name translation, name mapping or address resolution; don’t confuse it with ARP, which maps IP addresses to MAC addresses). Why use names at all? Because IP addresses are hard to remember : people remember google.com, not 142.250.185.46. Names also stay the same when a server moves to a new address. The problem is that the network itself only understands numeric addresses . The solution: let people use alphanumeric names, and add a distributed, hierarchical protocol, DNS, that maps between names and IP addresses whenever a program needs to contact a host. IP addresses are unique, so host names must be unique too. With billions of hosts, one flat list of names would be impossible to manage. The solution: each name is made of several parts, and each part is called a label . The names form a tree with the root at the top : this is the hierarchical name space . Name resolution

DNS is a client-server application. The client part is the resolver ; the server part is the name server (whose host name typically starts with the label “DNS”, as in DNS.psu.edu.sa). The resolver receives a request from an application-layer program (such as HTTP) as a system call, and returns the answer in a format the local host can use. There are two ways to resolve a name. The first is recursive resolution : host A asks its local name server B. If B has the answer in its cache or database, it replies. Otherwise B asks a root server; if the root doesn’t know, it asks a server at the next level (C) itself, and so on down the tree until some server has the answer. The answer is then passed back along the same chain to host A. In recursive resolution, each server takes over the job of finding the answer for the one that asked it. Recursive resolution: example

The example: host lab.CS.PSU.EDU.SA wants the IP address of the web server Sales.mcgraw.com. In steps 1 to 4 the query is passed along: the host asks DNS.PSU.EDU.SA, which asks the root, which asks DNS.com, which asks DNS.mcgraw.com. In steps 5 to 8 the answer comes back the same way, server by server, to the host. 1- Recursive resolution – Example (cont’d.)

The steps in words: (1) the host asks its local name server , DNS.PSU.EDU.SA. (2) It doesn’t know, so it asks the root server. (3) The root doesn’t know, so the root asks DNS.com. (4) DNS.com doesn’t know, so it asks DNS.McGraw.com , which has the answer. (5–8) DNS.McGraw.com answers DNS.com, which answers the root, which answers the local server, which answers the host. The key point: each server asks the next one on behalf of the server that asked it. In RECURSIVE resolution for sales.mcgraw.com from lab.CS.PSU.EDU.SA, who contacts DNS.com? In the recursive example, which server finally has the answer? 1- Recursive resolution – Example (cont’d.) In the previous example, the mapping will be done as follows: 1- Host lab.CS.PSU.EDU.SA contacts the local name server (DNS.PSU.EDU.SA) to query for the IP address of web server sales.McGraw.com 2- If (DNS.PSU.EDU.SA) does not have the answer in its cache or in its database, it will contact the root name server to query for the IP address of web server sales.McGraw.com 3- If the root name server does not have the answer in its cache or in its database, it will contact the name server responsible for the .com domain (DNS.com ) to query for the IP address of web server sales.McGraw.com 4- If (DNS.com) does not have the answer in its cache or in its database, it will contact (DNS.McGraw.com) which has the IP address for web server (Sales.McGraw.com) 5- (DNS.McGraw.com) will return the answer to (DNS.com) 6- (DNS.com) will return the answer to the root name server 7- The root name server will return the answer to (DNS.PSU.EDU.SA) 8- DNS.PSU.EDU.SA will return the answer to Host lab.CS.PSU.EDU.SA McGraw-Hill
2- Iterative resolution (mapping)

The second technique is iterative resolution . Host A asks its local name server B. If B doesn’t have the answer, it asks a root server. But this time, a root server that doesn’t know the answer doesn’t ask anyone else. It replies to B with the IP address of the name server at the next level (C): in effect, “I don’t know, ask C”. The local name server B then sends its query directly to C, and the process repeats: each server either answers or gives B the address of the next one, until B gets the IP address that was asked for. Finally B sends the answer to host A. The difference from recursive: in iterative resolution the local server does all the asking , and the other servers only give referrals. Memory aid: recursive = “I’ll find out for you”; iterative = “ask him instead”. Recursive = “I’ll find out for you.” Iterative = “Ask him instead.” In iterative resolution the root never contacts DNS.com; it only tells the local server where DNS.com is. In iterative resolution, the root server answers the local server with: Compare recursive and iterative DNS resolution. In iterative resolution, the root server contacts DNS.com on the local server’s behalf. 2- Iterative resolution (mapping) ▪ Host A sends a query to local name server B ▪ If B has the answer in its cache or in its database, it returns it to A, otherwise it send requests to one of the root name servers ▪ The root name server (if it does not have the answer in its cache or in its database) sends a reply to B that contains the IP address of name server in the next level of the tree say ( C ) ▪ Local name server B then sends a query directly to name server C ▪ The process is repeated until local name server B received the IP address for the requested mapping ▪ Local name server B then sends the answer to Host A ▪ SEE the next example McGraw-Hill

The same lookup done iteratively: the local server DNS.PSU.EDU.SA queries the root (steps 2–3), which refers it to DNS.com; it then queries DNS.com (4–5), which refers it to DNS.mcgraw.com; it then queries DNS.mcgraw.com (6–7), which gives the answer; and it answers the host (8). Every arrow starts or ends at the local server : the root never talks to DNS.com. The steps in words: (1) the host asks the local server. (2) The local server asks the root . (3) The root replies with the address of DNS.com . (4) The local server asks DNS.com . (5) DNS.com replies with the address of DNS.McGraw.com . (6) The local server asks DNS.McGraw.com . (7) DNS.McGraw.com, being responsible for McGraw.com, replies with the IP address of sales.McGraw.com . (8) The local server gives it to the host. So the local server sent three queries itself (root, DNS.com, DNS.McGraw.com). In the iterative example, which server sends the query to DNS.McGraw.com? Note: DNS ports

DNS can use either UDP or TCP , on the well-known port 53 . Normal lookups use UDP , because a query and its answer are each short enough to fit in one datagram (Chapter 9); TCP is used for large transfers such as zone transfers between primary and secondary servers.
